rationale: The two candidates are near-clones: same angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=30,750) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model C-index). With design and endpoint fidelity indistinguishable, the only differentiator is the selected European full-model C-index, which is trivially higher for PGS005048 (0.76688 vs 0.76625 for PGS005052), while OR per SD is essentially the same (1.487 vs 1.491). Given the minimal and likely-noise metric gap, confidence is low but PGS005048 gets the slight edge on the only performance field that differs.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, so phenotype fidelity doesn’t separate them. PGS001267 provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265; PGS-only R2=0.0988) with only basic covariates, and its PRS-only R2 is plausible under the provided liability h2 ceiling (0.399). In contrast, PGS002089 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive strength less directly supported/comparable despite a larger variant count and training N. Given the benchmark goal and the stronger, directly PRS-isolated metric evidence, PGS001267 is better-supported here.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis: its trait_reported/trait_efo are directly aortic stenosis and phenotyping_reported is incident aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is framed as “Mean pressure gradient” with trait_efo including aortic measurement (more proxy/measurement-like despite the same incident AS phenotyping). Both are near-clones otherwise (same paper, PRS-CS, EUR-only dev/eval, same covariates, same validation N), so tie-breakers are effect size and overall coherence: PGS005254 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53) and has a larger training sample (205,483 vs 98,645), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either to override these signals.

PGS001344 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance for asthma: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.64568 and PGS-only R²=0.05973 (with CIs for AUROC) under basic covariates, and the PRS-only R² is plausibly below the asthma liability h² ceiling (~0.15). PGS002061 comes from a portability framework and, while it uses a stronger genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with many more variants and larger training N, it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² entirely and only provides partial correlation (partial-r=0.1184), which is harder to benchmark against typical PRS discrimination. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (asthma diagnosis), and validation Ns are similar, so the decisive visible advantage is PGS001344’s clean PRS-only metrics versus PGS002061’s less directly comparable metric reporting.

PGS001268 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported for ankylosing spondylitis (PGS-only AUROC=0.7346; PGS-only R2=0.10232) with only basic covariates, and its PRS-only R2 is plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.399), making the metric interpretable. PGS002089 matches the endpoint label well and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, but it provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and only a partial correlation (0.0919), which is harder to benchmark against the other candidate’s PRS-only metrics. Both are UKB framework-style scores; given that, the cleaner, directly PRS-only discrimination evidence in PGS001268 is the stronger visible support despite its time-to-event framing and very sparse variant set.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric-asthma PRS study and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=1.57 per SD), which is a meaningful discriminator signal even though only a full-model AUROC (0.66) is shown and covariates are unknown. PGS002061 comes from a UKB portability/framework paper ("Portability of 245 polygenic scores"), which is systematically less reliable for external transfer when a disease-focused alternative exists; it also provides only a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.1184) and no effect-size/AUROC evidence. Despite PGS002061’s much larger training N and explicit basic covariates, the combination of disease-focused endpoint framing plus stronger effect-size evidence favors PGS002727.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003973 is better-supported structurally and by study context: it is a disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis score using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T 29-variant PGS000753. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model C-index=0.882 for PGS003973 (age/age^2/sex adjusted) cannot be treated as a standalone PRS metric, but its covariates are still basic and not an obvious leakage package. PGS000753 does provide an OR per SD of 1.37 (moderate signal) and has larger validation N, yet its extremely low variant count and simpler method are weaker structural evidence than PGS003973’s genome-wide construction and broader development cohorts.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance fields are not directly comparable. In that setting, study archetype and structural signals dominate: PGS003973 comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many contributing cohorts) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with larger variant coverage (~1.12M) and only basic covariates (age, age^2, sex), whereas PGS002054 is from a UKB portability/framework paper (single-biobank derivation) with only a weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r=0.0144) and heavier standard covariate adjustment (incl. PCs, deprivation, birth date). The very high full-model C-index (0.882) for PGS003973 is not treated as PRS-only evidence, but combined with the disease-focused design and broader development context it is better-supported than the portability score.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication/study family, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distributions, and same validation size (n=30,750). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index differences are weak. As a tie-break within this same-context sibling pair, PGS005048 shows marginally stronger empirical signals (slightly higher full-model C-index 0.76688 vs 0.76637 and slightly higher OR per SD 1.487 vs 1.479), so it is the better-supported pick, but the advantage is very small.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait sparse snpnet framework paper, with identical training cohort/size (UKB n=269,704), variant count (10), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and the same selected European validation context (n=67,425). Candidate_b (PGS001268) has slightly higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346 vs 0.7265; PGS-only R2 0.1023 vs 0.0988), but it is explicitly a time-to-event endpoint (phenotyping_reported: TTE ankylosing spondylitis), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity mismatch for a generic ‘ankylosing spondylitis’ target compared with candidate_a’s direct disease endpoint. Given the tiny performance gap and the endpoint-fidelity preference, PGS001267 is marginally better-supported, though the decision is close.

PGS004913 is better-supported for the target endpoint: its trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both directly match alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis, whereas PGS001777’s phenotyping_reported is “Cirrhosis (males)”, introducing a sex-restricted framing that is less faithful to the generic target. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R², so PGS001777’s reported AUROC=0.671 is a full-model metric and not a clean PRS-comparable advantage (and its covariates are unknown). With metrics largely non-comparable, structural/study signals matter more: PGS004913 is a dedicated PRSice-2 score with more variants (20 vs 3) and explicitly basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), suggesting a more standard PRS construction and evaluation than the older 3-variant genetic risk score in PGS001777.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: M13 Other arthritis; trait_efo: arthritis), study family (same Commun Biol paper), ancestry (EUR-only dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), training N and validation N, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (no pgs_only metrics). With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available PRS signal proxy: candidate_b reports a higher per-SD odds ratio (OR=1.262) than candidate_a (OR=1.196), suggesting stronger discriminative power in the same context. Method differences are secondary here, but candidate_b’s metaPRS-style aggregation is also structurally compatible with improved performance versus a single-score LDpred2 sibling. Therefore PGS004547 is better-supported.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable PRS metrics. Candidate_a (PGS005168) is heavily risk-wrapper packaged via the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in covariates, making its very high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and discounted for standalone PRS quality; it also reports HR=1.67 per SD but without clean PRS-only discrimination. Candidate_b (PGS005313) uses much cleaner covariates (age, sex only), reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.82) that is a meaningful PRS-strength signal, and uses a cross-ancestry shrinkage method (PRS-CSx) with substantially more variants (1.27M vs 0.38M), which is a positive structural indicator when PRS-only metrics are absent. Despite smaller validation N, the cleaner covariate design plus stronger OR and more powerful cross-ancestry construction make PGS005313 better-supported for external PRS performance.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). However, PGS000016 provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.029) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, chip), and that R2 is plausible relative to the AF heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.020–0.031). In contrast, PGS005168 reports only a full-model C-index (0.8718) while explicitly including the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in covariates, making the high discrimination likely covariate-packaged and not comparable as standalone PRS evidence despite its disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS context and supportive HR per SD (1.67). Given the strong penalty for clinical risk-calculator packaging and the lack of PRS-only metrics for PGS005168, PGS000016 is better-supported for benchmark-style PRS performance.

PGS002727 is better-supported for the target trait asthma because it is a disease-focused, endpoint-specific score for **pediatric asthma** developed in a dedicated asthma paper and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (~986k) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.57), plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS001344 comes from a known pan-trait UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a sparse snpnet model (6,139 variants), which domain guidance flags as often less transferable despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R² reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.646; R²=0.0597, below the asthma h2 ceiling). While PGS001344’s PRS-only metrics are a plus, the framework/sparse-model penalty and weaker disease-focused support make PGS002727 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates match the target trait well (AAA) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics don’t clearly separate them. PGS000753 is from a disease-focused AAA genetic-architecture study (MVP/Mayo-VDB) with a direct clinical endpoint (“Prevalent abdominal aortic aneurysm”) and provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.37, 95% CI 1.30–1.44), which is meaningful PRS signal evidence in the absence of PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS002054 comes from a UKB portability framework paper (explicitly a cross-trait portability sweep archetype) and only provides a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0144), which is weak and less directly interpretable for discrimination; despite its genome-wide LDpred2 construction and large training N, the framework context is a negative signal when a disease-focused alternative exists. Covariates are basic in both (PGS002054 slightly heavier but still demographic/PC), so the main differentiator is disease-focused evidence + OR support (PGS000753) versus portability-framework + weak partial-r (PGS002054).

PGS004587 is better aligned to the target trait as a general atopic eczema/atopic dermatitis endpoint (phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis), whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis), which is a partial endpoint mismatch for generic atopic eczema. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high reported AUROC/R² are full-model metrics with covariates including parental ethnicity (risk of covariate-driven inflation and non-comparability), and its R²=0.49 is implausibly above the eczema heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.07; h2_liab≈0.13), further discounting it as PRS evidence. PGS004587, while also sparse and lacking AUC/R², at least reports a PRS-stratified HR (1.153 high vs low) in a large EUR evaluation (n=337,910) with relatively standard covariates, making it the more credible, better-supported choice here.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported incident atopic dermatitis), use the same covariates, and have the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so metrics don’t cleanly differentiate. The structural/model-quality signals favor PGS002755: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to capturing polygenic signal than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNPs. The available effect-size evidence is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR high vs low 1.249 vs 1.153). While PGS004587 lists multiple training cohorts (EB/FinnGen/UKB), its sparse GWS-only construction and weaker HR make it less likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the genome-wide shrinkage model.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with very large variant count (326,000) and shows a stronger top-decile enrichment (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (1.76 [1.32–2.34]), suggesting better discrimination. PGS002739 is a gene-based PRS-CSx model with only 858 variants and is evaluated only in AFR; while valuable for African-ancestry deployment, the sparse gene-based construction and weaker OR provide less support for higher overall benchmark ranking than the more genome-wide PGS002738.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is a direct clinical diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence) and it shows stronger PRS signal in the reported effect metrics (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76; β=0.17). It is also developed from multiple cohorts (MVP/PGC/UKB) and uses a cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with AFR evaluation (n=6,315), which is supportive for robustness beyond a single-biobank EUR-only setting. In contrast, PGS000201 is less endpoint-faithful (trait_reported: Problematic alcohol use; trait_efo: alcohol dependence measurement) and its only comparable performance evidence is a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192 with covariate adjustment, offering weaker direct evidence of PRS discrimination for alcohol dependence despite its large variant count and slightly larger EUR validation sample.

PGS001135 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence and endpoint transparency: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC=0.539, R2=0.00291) with basic covariates and these are sanity-consistent with the low heritability ceiling, whereas PGS004477 provides no AUROC/R2 at all (only OR=1.20) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive performance and comparability hard to judge. Although PGS004477 uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score with many variants (a structural plus) and a larger validation N, the lack of PRS-only performance metrics and unclear covariate/packaging context outweigh that advantage versus the clearly quantified (if modest) PRS signal in PGS001135.

PGS004913 is the better-supported match for the target because it is explicitly disease-focused on alcohol-associated cirrhosis in heavy drinkers with coherent endpoint fields (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis) and provides PRS-relevant effect evidence (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). PGS000704, while much larger and genome-wide, comes from a broad UKB biomarker genetics framework context and reports only a full-model C-index (0.711) plus a modest HR=1.18, with no PRS-only AUC/R2; its apparent performance is therefore less directly attributable to the PRS and less endpoint-optimized for alcoholic cirrhosis than the dedicated cirrhosis PRS study.

PGS002755 is better-supported for the target trait (atopic eczema) as a general atopic dermatitis PRS: its endpoint is closer to the broad target (phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis; trait_reported: atopic dermatitis) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than PGS001773’s 25-variant hit score. While PGS001773 reports a very high AUROC/R², these are full-model metrics (not PRS-only) and are paired with covariates including parental ethnicity, making the discrimination less interpretable as standalone PRS performance; additionally its phenotype is restricted to moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (a narrower subtype than the target). PGS002755 lacks PRS-only AUC/R², but it provides a PRS effect size (HR high vs low PRS 1.249) in a very large European evaluation (n=337,910), and avoids relying on an implausibly high full-model AUROC as evidence of PRS strength.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation). PGS005313 is better-supported as a disease-focused, multi-cohort, cross-population development (AFGen, BBJ, FinnGen, MVP, UKB, deCODE, etc.) with multi-ancestry GWAS input and explicitly broad evaluation ancestries, and it shows strong PRS signal via an OR=1.82 per SD. PGS000016 has a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.029, below the AF h2_obs ceiling ~0.020–0.031 range but plausible on that scale) and a much larger EUR validation sample, but it is essentially a single-biobank (UKB) development from a pan-disease framework paper and lacks effect-size evidence here. Given domain guidance that disease-focused multi-cohort scores typically outperform framework-derived UKB scores unless the framework has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence, PGS005313 is the more likely external-transfer winner despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it is explicitly labeled and mapped to aortic stenosis and uses an incident aortic stenosis endpoint, whereas PGS005255 is framed as “Mean pressure gradient” with an EFO that includes aortic measurement, making endpoint fidelity less direct despite also mentioning incident aortic stenosis. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size and design signals matter more; PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting stronger standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252 reports a high full-model C-index (0.87), it is paired with a much heavier clinical covariate set (comorbidities and risk factors), so that metric is not treated as PRS-comparable; still, the stronger HR and cleaner trait alignment outweigh PGS005255’s larger training N and simpler covariates.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (aortic stenosis) with incident-case endpoints and EUR-only development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so PGS005252’s full-model C-index=0.87 is not a comparable PRS metric, especially given its heavy clinical covariate set). The main differentiators are (i) cleaner covariate design and (ii) effect-size evidence: PGS005254 adjusts only for basic demographics/PCs (age, age^2, sex, PCs), making its HR per SD (1.64, 95% CI 1.50–1.78) more interpretable as PRS signal, whereas PGS005252 includes multiple comorbidities/risk factors (T2D, HTN, CAD, hyperlipidemia, BMI, smoking, renal failure) that can soak up risk and make reported metrics less comparable. While PGS005252 shows a higher HR (1.92) and larger validation N, the lack of CI and the covariate-heavy modeling reduce confidence that this reflects stronger standalone PRS performance. Overall, PGS005254 is better-supported as a cleaner disease-risk PRS for benchmarking.

Both candidates map to the broad target (trait_efo=arthritis), but PGS001135 is a pan-trait UKB sparse-score from the “813 traits” framework and shows very weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.539, PGS-only R2 0.00291), suggesting limited standalone signal despite clean basic covariates. PGS004547 is more disease-focused in framing (“Other arthritis”) and uses an explicit meta/ensemble-style approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with genome-wide scale variant count (~1.06M) and reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.26), which—despite missing AUC/R2 and unknown covariates—provides at least some evidence of discriminative utility and avoids the known underperformance pattern of the UKB pan-trait sparse framework. Given the extremely low PRS-only metrics for PGS001135, PGS004547 is more likely to rank higher, but confidence is low due to PGS004547’s missing comparable PRS metrics.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS000704 has stronger structural support for a polygenic predictor: a genome-wide snpnet model with 183,271 variants trained in UKB (n=223,327) and evaluated in a large sample (n=135,300) with basic covariates (age as timescale, sex, batch, PCs). PGS001777 is a very sparse 3-variant score (“Variants associated with alcohol related cirrhosis”) with unknown covariates and its only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC (0.671) in a smaller evaluation (n=1,390), plus an extreme tail OR that is harder to compare across designs. Since neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, the more robust genome-wide construction and larger, cleaner evaluation context of PGS000704 outweigh PGS001777’s disease-focused paper framing.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both “Alcohol use disorder” and trait_efo maps to “alcohol dependence,” whereas PGS000201 is framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo “alcohol dependence measurement,” making it more measurement/proxy-like despite a DSM-5 criteria-count phenotype. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparison relies on available effect-size evidence: PGS002738 reports a reasonably strong risk stratification (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96), while PGS000201 only shows a small incremental ΔR² (0.01192) alongside a beta on a transformed count outcome, which is harder to interpret as disease-risk discrimination. Study/transport context is also slightly stronger for PGS002738 (multi-cohort development: MVP + UKB, and multi-ancestry GWAS input) versus PGS000201 (UKB-only GWAS), with similar EUR-only evaluation sizes.

Both candidates are near-clones: same angina pectoris PheCode 411.3 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and release date, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,750), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index ~0.766, which is not a PRS-comparable metric). With design and metric comparability essentially identical, the only meaningful differentiator is effect size: PGS005052 has a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.479 for PGS005057), while the tiny full-model C-index difference (0.76625 vs 0.76637) is negligible. Therefore PGS005052 is marginally better-supported, but confidence is low due to the minimal differences.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder) at the concept level (trait_reported/trait_efo both bipolar disorder), whereas PGS002787 targets the narrower subtype bipolar I disorder. Neither candidate provides PRS-comparable metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R2; only small partial R² values in a non-disease endpoint context), and both share the same method (SDPR), training cohort (PGC), and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, so the slightly higher partial R² for PGS002787 is not a reliable differentiator. Given near-tie evidence, endpoint/concept alignment favors PGS002786.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates, training size, and evaluation ancestry/validation N, and they show essentially identical partial-r (0.0563 vs 0.0562). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes to separate them, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (32,552) versus PGS001826’s very sparse penalized regression score (45 variants). Given the same context and indistinguishable observed partial-r, the higher-coverage shrinkage model is better-supported to generalize and capture polygenic signal.

PGS001263 is the better match to the target trait (atrial flutter) with direct trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all specific to atrial flutter, whereas PGS001339 targets a broader combined endpoint (atrial fibrillation and flutter) and is explicitly time-to-event (TTE), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic atrial flutter target. The two scores are near-clones otherwise (same snpnet method, same UKB-only framework paper, same training N, same covariates, same validation N and selected EUR validation), so PRS-only performance can be used as a tie-break: PGS001263 has slightly higher PGS-only AUROC (0.61716 vs 0.613) and PGS-only R2 (0.02517 vs 0.02447), both plausible under the heritability ceiling. Overall, the more endpoint-faithful model with marginally better PRS-only metrics wins.

PGS000327 is far better aligned to the target endpoint: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Autism spectrum disorder,” matching trait_reported/trait_efo, whereas PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch (“Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”) despite the ASD label fields, making its validation metric less relevant to ASD risk prediction. PGS000327 also comes from a disease-focused ASD GWAS meta-analysis context (Nat Genet; multiple ASD cohorts listed) and provides a meaningful PRS signal via an OR=1.33 per SD and higher reported R² (0.0245) than PGS002790’s small partial R² (~0.0055) from a cross-psychiatric/cognition study with unclear training sample size (N/A). Although PGS002790 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, the endpoint/phenotype incoherence and weaker reported association outweigh that structural advantage.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and size (n=11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation size (n=11,322), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not strong cross-model differentiators here). With endpoints and context effectively identical, the small full-model AUROC/R² edge favors candidate_a (PGS000454: AUROC 0.632, Nagelkerke R² 0.0489) over candidate_b (PGS000456: AUROC 0.630, R² 0.0456), while candidate_b’s slightly higher top-1% OR does not clearly outweigh that. Given the tiny metric differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo align directly with bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the narrower bipolar II subtype (trait_efo: bipolar II disorder), which is a phenotype mismatch for a generic bipolar disorder benchmark. Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts, identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (age, PCs1-3), and the same validation sample size (n=2,524), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the slightly higher partial R² in PGS002788 (0.00307 vs 0.00251) is weak and not clearly comparable to a disease-risk PRS benchmark given both are evaluated on non-disease phenotypes (cognition/behavior). With near-clone study context otherwise, endpoint fidelity to bipolar disorder favors PGS002786.

PGS001824 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported are specifically “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease), whereas PGS000924 is a broader combined phenotype (“disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism”) and is explicitly time-to-event, which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease target. Although PGS000924 reports strong-looking PRS-only AUROC/R², its PRS-only R² (0.218) exceeds the provided local heritability ceiling for bilirubin (~0.089), making the metric suspect/non-comparable on the visible evidence. PGS001824 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² but provides a modest partial-r and comes from a portability evaluation with multi-ancestry EVAL, so on balance the more coherent phenotype match and the heritability-sanity issue in PGS000924 tip the decision to PGS001824.

PGS001033 is the better-supported match to the target trait "blood coagulation disease" because its trait_efo is exactly blood coagulation disease and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.634 and PGS-only R²=0.0578) with only basic covariates. PGS001826 targets a narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency subtype (trait_efo: congenital vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors deficiency), which is a phenotype mismatch for the broader target, and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a modest partial correlation is shown), making its predictive strength harder to benchmark. Although both come from UKB framework-style papers, the combination of exact endpoint alignment plus explicit PRS-only metrics favors PGS001033.

Both candidates target the same combined endpoint (atrial fibrillation and flutter) with similar basic covariates and UKB-only development, so endpoint fidelity is essentially tied for the atrial flutter target. PGS004254, while lacking PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC reported), is built with a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) using far more variants (744,682) and reports a strong effect size (OR 2.18), which is supportive of materially better PRS discrimination than the weak PRS-only metrics in PGS001331. Given the framework-penalty and low PRS-only signal for PGS001331, PGS004254 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks despite less directly comparable AUC/R² reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates, training cohort (UKB), training N, ancestry distribution, publication family, and validation size—so the decision rests on within-family structural/performance differences. PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally a positive structural signal for complex disease PRS in the absence of clean PRS-only AUC/R2 for either model. It also has a slightly higher partial correlation (0.0797 vs 0.0783), albeit a small gap. With no other differentiators, the combination of much larger variant set plus marginally better partial-r supports PGS002092 over the sparse penalized-regression score PGS001880.

PGS004254 is more likely to rank higher because it is a disease-focused Crohn’s disease PRS (Nat Commun) built with a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) and very large variant count (744,682), and it reports a strong effect size signal (OR=2.18, 95% CI 2.05–2.32) in EUR evaluation—consistent with meaningful PRS discrimination. In contrast, PGS001330 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very small SNP set (220) and correspondingly weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.576; PGS-only R2 0.0062), despite larger training N; its time-to-event phenotyping framing is also a mild endpoint mismatch for generic Crohn’s disease risk. Although PGS004254 lacks explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only full-model AUROC=0.72), its strong OR plus structurally stronger genome-wide construction outweigh the framework/sparse/low-metric evidence for PGS001330.

PGS004951 is better aligned to the target trait as a generic dilated cardiomyopathy PRS (phenotyping_reported: “Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”), whereas PGS004949 is explicitly restricted to “Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy,” a subtype mismatch for the broader target. Both are near-clone siblings (same paper, PRS-CS, similar variant counts, similar PRS-only AUC ~0.67–0.68 and OR ~1.9), so endpoint fidelity is the main differentiator. Although PGS004949 has a much larger validation sample and slightly higher PRS-only AUC, it also uses a heavier covariate set and its subtype framing reduces generalizability to the broad DCM benchmark setting; PGS004951’s cleaner covariates and broader clinical endpoint make it the safer, better-supported choice.

PGS004949 is better-supported on PRS-relevant evidence: it reports an explicit PRS-only (univariate) AUC of 0.68 (with CI) plus PRS contribution metrics (delta pseudo-R² and delta liability-scale R²), and it shows a slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.91 vs 1.76 for PGS004862). Both candidates are MTAG DCM PRS-CS scores with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), so covariate leakage concerns are low and comparable. While PGS004862 has cleaner endpoint wording (phenotyping_reported exactly ‘Dilated cardiomyopathy’) and EUR-only evaluation, its performance evidence is mainly full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) without PRS-only metrics, making it less directly comparable for PRS strength than PGS004949’s PRS-isolated reporting. The non-ischemic DCM phenotyping in PGS004949 is a mild endpoint narrowing but not enough to outweigh the stronger PRS-specific metric support.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to COPD (candidate_a uses ICD10 J44; candidate_b uses generic COPD), and both are evaluated in EUR. Candidate_b (PGS001788) provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.0163), which is plausible under the provided COPD h2_obs ceiling (~0.0122) but close enough to raise mild scale/comparability uncertainty; its AUROC=0.715 is full-model and not PRS-only. Candidate_a (PGS004536) lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, but it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.49), near the “strong” threshold and more indicative of meaningful PRS discrimination than candidate_b’s modest R2 alone. Structurally, candidate_a is a meta/ensemble-style score (RFDiseasemetaPRS integrating risk-factor PRS with disease PRS) with higher variant count (1,059,939 vs 910,082), which is a positive signal when not obviously clinically packaged; candidate_b comes from a known global biobank portability/framework paper, which is typically less optimized per-disease unless it has clearly superior PRS-only performance evidence. Given the stronger effect-size evidence plus favorable structural signals, PGS004536 is better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only R2/AUC.

PGS004614 is the stronger pick because it is disease-focused with a direct diverticular disease endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (SBayesR) with very broad variant coverage (1,082,282 SNPs), plus multi-ancestry evaluation is indicated. PGS000997, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC=0.591, PGS R2=0.0178) and large UKB training/validation, comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event framing and a very sparse snpnet model (5,757 SNPs), which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external transfer than a disease-focused genome-wide score. PGS004614’s reported AUROC=0.76 is full-model and includes family history (covariate leakage concern), so confidence is not high, but overall study archetype + method/coverage favor PGS004614 over the framework sparse alternative.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported and trait_efo are all-cause dementia/dementia). However, PGS005170 is better-supported as a transferable dementia PRS: it is an explicit multi-score integrative PRS (24 component PRSs; >1.3M variants), evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR) and reports a PRS-linked effect size (HR=1.25 per SD), giving at least some direct evidence of genetic discrimination beyond covariates. PGS004281 is a single-biobank UKB-only GenoBoost model with a very small variant set (110) and only full-model metrics (AUROC ~0.819, pseudo-R2 ~0.034) that are not PRS-only; with no effect sizes and EUR-only evaluation, its apparent performance advantage is likely more covariate/internal-setting driven and less informative for standalone PRS ranking. Given both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, the structural and transportability advantages favor PGS005170.

Both candidates target the same trait framing ("Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)") with PRS-CS and EUR evaluation, so endpoint alignment is broadly comparable; candidate_b is slightly more explicitly clinical in phenotyping ("Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy") vs candidate_a ("Dilated cardiomyopathy"). The key differentiator is that PGS004951 reports PRS-comparable performance evidence (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101) plus a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.93) while staying below the heritability ceiling, whereas PGS004862 provides only full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) without isolating PRS contribution and a weaker OR (1.76). Although PGS004862 has a much larger validation sample and slightly cleaner/basic covariates, those are weak signals and its AUROC is not PRS-only; overall the direct PRS-only metrics and stronger effect size make PGS004951 better-supported for expected benchmark ranking.

PGS000997 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence for diverticular disease: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC=0.591 and PRS-only R²=0.0178 (with CIs for AUROC) under basic covariates, and its PRS-only R² is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (~0.0174–0.0229). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (EUR plus AFR/EAS/SAS) and clearly specified covariates, reducing ambiguity about leakage. PGS004544 has an endpoint-aligned ICD10 K57 phenotype and a moderate OR=1.32, but provides no AUC/R² at all and has unknown covariates; additionally, it is a risk-factor integration/metaPRS-style model, which raises packaging/comparability uncertainty without accompanying PRS-only metrics. Given the missing performance detail and covariate opacity for PGS004544, PGS000997 is the more reliably supported choice despite being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and diagnosis-like phenotyping_reported). PGS001254 is better-supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.6646 and PGS-only R²=0.0247 in European evaluation, whereas PGS001880 provides no PRS-only AUC/R² and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0783), which is harder to benchmark against other PRS metrics. Although PGS001880 has a larger variant set (2443 vs 11) and multi-ancestry evaluation context, the lack of standard PRS-only discrimination/variance metrics makes its expected benchmark ranking less certain than PGS001254’s quantified PRS-only performance.

PGS002304 has the cleanest endpoint fidelity to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000644 is labeled “Nodular lymphoma” in both fields (despite mapping to the same EFO), introducing avoidable phenotype ambiguity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS002304 shows higher AUROC (0.61 vs 0.538) in European evaluation. Although PGS000644 has a stronger genome-wide method (lassosum; ~2.2M variants) and basic covariates disclosed, its reported effect size is modest (OR per SD ~1.15) and the phenotype labeling mismatch makes it less well-supported for follicular lymphoma specifically. Overall, the direct phenotype match plus better observed discrimination favors PGS002304.

PGS004614 is better supported for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it is clearly disease-focused (publication explicitly on diverticular disease risk variants and prediction) with direct phenotype alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and it provides at least one concrete discrimination result (full-model AUROC 0.76 with CI) plus evidence of evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/SAS), suggesting some robustness beyond EUR-only. PGS004544 matches the ICD10 K57 endpoint but comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”), has unknown covariates (raising comparability uncertainty), and provides no AUC/R2 at all—only a moderate OR per SD (~1.32). With both lacking PRS-only metrics, the stronger endpoint-focused study context and the available discrimination evidence favor PGS004614.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and direct disease phenotyping). PGS001254 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6646; PGS R2 0.0247) but comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant snpnet model, a pattern associated with poorer external transfer. PGS002092, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score with very large variant coverage (484,484) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability support than EUR-only evaluation. Given the framework+sparsity warning for PGS001254 and the broader, genome-wide + multi-ancestry evaluation context for PGS002092, PGS002092 is better-supported to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target/phenotype (gout), same publication family, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (6,704), same eval ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) and validation N (90,274), and both list covariates as 0 with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported—so we must use within-family performance/effect-size differences. PGS004160 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) shows consistently stronger reported discrimination than PGS004047 (LDpred2.CV): higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.685), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.080), and slightly higher OR per SD (2.05 vs 2.00). Given identical endpoint and evaluation context, the ensemble/multi-PRS structure plus the modest but consistent metric edge supports PGS004160 as more likely to rank higher externally.

Both candidates have clean endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all = gout). However, PGS004047 provides substantially stronger direct evidence of PRS discriminative signal via effect sizes (OR per SD ≈ 2.0 with tight CI) and multiple validation records, plus evaluation beyond EUR (EUR+SAS), suggesting better-supported transportability. PGS004768 reports only an incremental R2/full-model delta (0.081) with no PRS-only metrics and no effect sizes, making its performance evidence less directly attributable to the PRS despite a larger variant count and larger training N. Given the stronger PRS-relevant evidence package in PGS004047, it is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. In this same-study, same-endpoint setting, the best available tie-break is the stronger observed association/performance: PGS005271 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and stronger effect sizes (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; β 0.438 vs 0.349) than PGS005272, with essentially identical variant count. Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same Cancer PRSweb paper with identical endpoint fields (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Nodular lymphoma; trait_efo = follicular lymphoma), identical EUR-only ancestry, same training cohort (MGI), same training n (3,696), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation n (3,256). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; the small full-model AUROC difference slightly favors PGS000644 (0.538 vs 0.532) and its per-SD OR is marginally higher (1.149 vs 1.133), while PGS000643 only stands out on the top-1% vs rest OR (2.49 vs 1.48). Given the otherwise identical context and lack of PRS-only metrics, I pick PGS000644 on the modestly stronger overall discrimination signals, but confidence is low because differences are small and CIs overlap.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Gout/gout”) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model metrics are not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. PGS004160 has stronger PRS-relevant empirical support via reported effect sizes (OR per SD ≈2.05 with tight CI), which is a meaningful discriminative signal when PRS-only metrics are absent, whereas PGS004768 provides no effect sizes and only an incremental R² figure that is harder to interpret cross-study. Although PGS004768 has larger training n and more variants, those are weaker predictors than having direct PRS signal evidence; additionally PGS004160’s evaluation includes both EUR and SAS (some breadth) with a much larger validation sample, supporting robustness. Overall, PGS004160 is better-supported on the visible fields for likely external performance.

PGS004944 is the better-supported glaucoma PRS here because it is more endpoint-faithful to the target (trait_efo=open-angle glaucoma and phenotyping_reported explicitly notes primary open-angle glaucoma, albeit self-reported) and it provides strong PRS signal evidence via an OR=1.74 per SD, which is a strong discriminative indicator even without PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS001792 does report a clean PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.03209), but it comes from a portability/framework-style ‘Global Biobank analyses…’ paper and has broader/less specific trait mapping (trait_efo=glaucoma) plus a modest R2; its full-model AUROC (0.777) is not PRS-comparable. With both lacking PRS-only AUROC and given the framework penalty, the stronger effect-size evidence and tighter phenotype mapping favor PGS004944, though confidence is low because PGS004944’s reported AUROC is full-model only and its phenotype is self-reported.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (good match to heart failure), same EFO mapping, same phenotyping, same covariates (age/sex/20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=31,804) with only full-model C-index reported (no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either). With design and comparability essentially identical, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005083 shows a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75325) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.455 vs 1.443). These are marginal, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS005083.

PGS000643 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for follicular lymphoma because it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score (~1,048,780 variants) with basic, explicitly stated covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs) and includes PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.133; top 1% vs rest OR 2.49) plus additional metrics (pseudo-R², Brier). PGS002304 has perfect endpoint fidelity (follicular lymphoma) but is an extremely sparse 6-variant GWS score with unknown covariates and provides only a full-model AUROC (0.61) on a very small validation set (n=197), which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven. Given both lack PRS-only AUC/R², the stronger methodological properties and richer PRS-specific performance evidence favor PGS000643 despite its less exact reported label ('nodular lymphoma').

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication/study family (HGG Adv benchmarking paper), same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions and validation size (n=31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are tiny performance/effect-size differences: PGS005083 has a marginally higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75358) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.455 vs 1.452). These differences are extremely small, so confidence is low, but they weakly favor PGS005083.

PGS001792 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence and broader external-transport context. It reports a PRS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.03209 (with basic covariates) in a large evaluation (n=347,396) and the value is plausible under the glaucoma heritability ceiling guidance, whereas PGS002761 provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 at all (only an OR=1.68) and has a much smaller evaluation sample (n=39,444). Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (POAG subtype vs generic glaucoma), but given the missing discrimination metrics for PGS002761 and the stronger multi-cohort, multi-ancestry development/validation framing for PGS001792, PGS001792 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), publication, evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%), and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.639 for PGS005270 vs 0.630 for PGS005271) is not a reliable differentiator. In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, structural and effect-size evidence matter more: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.55, β≈0.44) than PGS005270’s very sparse P+T 55-variant score with near-null effect (OR≈1.04, β≈0.04). That combination makes PGS005271 better-supported as a standalone PRS for Hashimoto’s/lymphocytic thyroiditis despite PGS005270’s slightly higher full-model AUROC.

PGS004944 is better supported for the target glaucoma context because it has higher endpoint fidelity (primary open-angle glaucoma / open-angle glaucoma with explicit self-reported POAG phenotyping) and substantially broader evaluation context (multi-ancestry validation listed and very large validation n=407,667) than PGS002761, which is a generic “Glaucoma” endpoint with only EUR evaluation (n=39,444) from a cross-disease comparison paper. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size and study/validation context: both have similar per-SD ORs (1.74 vs 1.68), but PGS004944’s slightly stronger OR plus broader validation support and disease-focused ocular phenotyping make it more likely to transfer well than the single-ancestry, sparse-metadata PGS002761.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), publication family, evaluation ancestry mix (MAE) and validation N (94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, structural signals and effect sizes matter more: PGS005272 uses PRSCS with genome-wide coverage (1,085,142 variants) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.42) than PGS005270 (OR≈1.04), which is consistent with better standalone PRS discrimination. The slightly higher full-model AUROC for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.605) is a small difference and not reliable for ranking without covariate details, so PGS005272 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint (Graves’ disease; strong match to hyperthyroidism), same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With design/endpoint/transportability effectively tied, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005265 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434), so it is marginally better-supported than PGS005266.

PGS004236 is from a disease-focused, multi-cohort, explicitly multi-ethnic hypertension study (BioMe/MVP/UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation and a strong reported PRS effect size (OR=2.1), which is supportive of meaningful standalone PRS discrimination even though it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R². PGS001320, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.629, R²=0.0649) and has large UKB training, is a pan-trait sparse UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”) that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer; its modest PRS-only performance and framework archetype make it less likely to rank highest in an external benchmark than the dedicated multi-ethnic hypertension PRS in PGS004236.

PGS002763 is the better-supported match for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is direct: phenotyping_reported is “Hip osteoarthritis,” aligning cleanly with the target, whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/surgical decision and disease severity rather than hip OA status. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either candidate, performance can’t be fairly compared via AUROC; PGS002728’s reported AUROC=0.66 is full-model with age/sex and is not a PRS-comparable metric. In that metric-absent setting, structural signals favor PGS002763: a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1,052,273 variants and a moderate per-SD OR=1.38 provides direct PRS discrimination evidence, while PGS002728 is a sparse 44-variant GWS score with no effect-size summary shown. Both are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL; PGS002763 also has a larger validation sample (39,444 vs 14,926), though this is only a weak tie-break.

The two candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported), same EFO mapping, same method (LDpred), identical variant count, same MVP development cohort, same covariates (age/sex/20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only show a full-model C-index, which is not a strong PRS-comparable differentiator here. With design effectively identical, the only visible tie-break is slightly stronger empirical signals for PGS005077 (higher full-model C-index 0.75358 vs 0.75325 and higher OR per SD 1.452 vs 1.443), so PGS005077 is marginally better-supported, but the difference is tiny hence low confidence.

PGS002763 is the better-supported match to the target trait hip osteoarthritis: its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are directly hip osteoarthritis, whereas PGS002750 is primarily a treatment/proxy endpoint (total hip replacement / hip replacement), which is a less faithful disease-status phenotype and can reflect access/clinical decision factors. With no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported for either candidate, effect-size and structural signals matter more: PGS002763 shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.38 vs 1.23) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS with ~1.05M variants) that is generally more appropriate for polygenic disease risk than a 37-SNP genome-wide-significant score. Both are EUR-only, but PGS002763 also has a much larger validation sample (39,444 vs 1,257), which mildly increases trust once endpoint fidelity is satisfied.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (Hodgkin's disease / Hodgkins lymphoma), cohorts (MGI), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this same-study, same-endpoint setting, the small full-model AUROC/R2 differences are at least a usable tie-break: PGS000638 shows slightly higher AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0193 vs 0.013) plus a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). Although PGS000637 is genome-wide (PRS-CS, 1,047,511 variants), its empirical performance signals here are weaker, so PGS000638 is marginally better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Commun paper with identical target trait (hypertension), identical phenotyping_reported (prevalent hypertension), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), and the same validation size/ancestry context (n=39,035; multi-ethnic evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.764 vs 0.763) is essentially noise and not a strong differentiator. In this tie-like setting, PGS004236 has better PRS-specific support: it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=2.1, 95% CI 1.99–2.21) whereas PGS004234 provides no effect size evidence, and it also uses a multi-score aggregation style method (PRSsum) with a larger variant set (398,805 vs 234,228), which is a mild structural advantage when endpoints/covariates are the same.

PGS004234 is from a disease-focused, hypertension-specific multi-ethnic study with explicit multi-ancestry development/validation (BioMe+UKB; DEV includes AFR/AMR/EUR/ASN; EVAL MAE), which is supportive for real-world transfer on a generic hypertension target. PGS001320, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649 below the h2 ceiling) and has much larger UKB training, is explicitly a pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a sparse snpnet model—an archetype that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable in external validation than disease-focused models. PGS004234’s reported AUROC (0.763) is full-model and covariate-influenced (age/sex/BMI/smoking etc.), so it can’t be used as PRS-only evidence, but the overall endpoint fidelity plus multi-cohort, multi-ancestry disease-focused design outweighs the framework-model metric advantage of PGS001320.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported Hodgkin’s disease; trait_efo Hodgkins lymphoma), same publication/family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training n=736, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on within-family performance/effect-size differences. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger signals than PGS000638: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher per-SD OR (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). Given identical design context, these differences favor PGS000639 as the better-supported score.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to depressive disorder (major depressive disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only show small full-model/unspecified R2 (~0.022 vs 0.0241), which is not cleanly comparable as standalone PRS performance. PGS003333 is better-supported as a disease-focused, multi-cohort-derived score (training_development_cohorts include 23andMe, PGC, UKB) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto), which is a positive structural signal for a highly polygenic trait. PGS003576 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and explicit PC covariates, but it appears developed from UKB only with a thresholding pipeline (PRSice-2), and its slightly higher reported R2 is too small and likely full-model to outweigh the structural/study-design advantage of PGS003333. Confidence is low because performance evidence is weak and non-PRS-comparable for both.

Both candidates are near-clones (same Nat Genet paper, PRS-CS, similar variant counts, identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates and cohorts, same validation n=343,182, and same phenotyping_reported = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC is only a weak tie-break. In this same-endpoint sibling comparison, PGS004911 has consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (higher full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; higher R² 0.048 vs 0.031; higher HR 2.34 vs 1.97; higher per-SD OR 1.33 vs 1.26; slightly higher high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced version, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base model when endpoint remains the same.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported (Hodgkin's disease), same EFO mapping (Hodgkins lymphoma), same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation sample size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on within-family empirical performance/effect sizes. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000637: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.3), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.67). Given identical covariates and endpoint framing, these differences are meaningful tie-breakers favoring PGS000639 despite PGS000637’s much larger variant count and PRS-CS method.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping (“Disorders of iron metabolism”), identical training size (n=391,124), covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation mix; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance evidence is limited to partial correlation. In this same-endpoint/same-study setting, PGS002031 has slightly stronger reported partial-r (0.1355 vs 0.1307) and is a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (6,713 vs 654), which is a favorable structural signal for a polygenic disease compared with the much sparser penalized regression score. The metric gap is small, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

PGS002728 is better supported for the target trait hip osteoarthritis because its endpoint framing is coherent with hip OA (trait_reported Hip osteoarthritis; phenotyping_reported total hip replacement as an advanced hip OA proxy) and it provides at least some discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.66 with only age/sex covariates), whereas PGS002750 is essentially the hip replacement endpoint but provides no AUC/R2 at all and only a modest per-SD OR (1.23), plus it uses a heavier covariate bundle (BMI, education, socioeconomic indices) that makes any unreported full-model performance less interpretable for PRS strength. Both are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL and similar GWAS-hit methods, but PGS002728 also has broader multi-cohort development listed and a much larger validation sample (14,926 vs 1,257), which mildly supports robustness when metrics are otherwise sparse.

PGS004910 is better-supported as a standalone HCM PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,190) and is evaluated in a large EUR sample (n=343,182) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), reducing risk that reported discrimination is driven by clinical-risk packaging. PGS000739 is a sparse 27-variant GWAS-hits score whose reported AUROC=0.821 is a full-model metric with heavy clinical covariates (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making that performance much less comparable to PRS-only utility and likely covariate-inflated. Both match the endpoint (HCM) and are Nat Genet disease-focused, but the cleaner covariate context and more polygenic model structure favor PGS004910 for external benchmark ranking.

PGS005265 is better-supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint is Graves’ disease (a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism) with coherent phenotype fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Graves’) and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-biobank, multi-ancestry study context (many cohorts; evaluation includes African American/Hispanic/European; large validation n=94,651). Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.665 is shown), it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.63), which is meaningful PRS signal. In contrast, PGS001043 is an older UKB pan-trait sparse-framework score (“across 813 traits”) with very few variants (69) and modest PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6323; R2=0.0216) that are consistent with limited standalone PRS signal; despite exact label match and clean covariates, the framework archetype and sparsity make it less likely to transfer well than the disease-focused Graves model.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity matches the umbrella disease: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly restricted to the oligoarticular subtype (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported), which is a phenotype mismatch for a generic JIA target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and EUR-only dev/eval, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000325 (0.80 vs 0.738) is discounted and not decisive. With comparable study context and no PRS-only metrics, the broader, directly aligned JIA score (PGS000114) is more likely to transfer to a benchmark defined on overall JIA rather than a single subtype.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (N18 chronic renal failure mapped to kidney failure), cohort context (UKB), ancestry (DEV/EVAL EUR only), variant count (1,059,939), training size (n=174,489), validation size (n=56,192), covariates (Unknown), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With metrics unavailable, the main differentiator is effect size: candidate_b (PGS004562) reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.39548; moderate) than candidate_a (PGS004492) OR 1.1708 (weak), suggesting better standalone PRS discrimination in the same study family/context. Method differences are secondary here, but candidate_b’s metaPRS-style aggregation is also structurally compatible with stronger performance than the single-score LDpred2 sibling.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) and shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) with a much larger variant set (107 vs 19). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown), so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.74 vs 0.722) is not a reliable differentiator; in that setting, the stronger per-SD effect size and richer disease-focused development context favor PGS004908 over PGS000076, which is from a cross-cancer evaluation paper and has a weaker HR per SD (1.16, 95% CI 1.08–1.26) despite similar covariate adjustment and EUR-only evaluation.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are EUR-trained/evaluated in UKB, with similar per-SD ORs (PGS004935 OR=1.50 vs PGS002766 OR=1.47). However, PGS004935’s only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.70 with covariates listed as Unknown, which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven; it provides limited standalone PRS evidence. PGS002766, while also lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, is built with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) and a much larger variant set (1,092,122 vs 6,127), a structural advantage for a polygenic disease when direct PRS-only metrics are absent. Given near-tied effect sizes and no PRS-only metrics for either, the stronger methodological/coverage signals favor PGS002766 despite PGS004935’s reported full-model AUROC.

PGS005218 is better supported as a hypothyroidism PRS because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with explicit large-scale multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and very large European evaluation (n=441,692), whereas PGS002766 is from a cross-disease “family history vs PRS across 24 diseases” framework-style paper with only UKB listed and much smaller evaluation (n=39,444). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS005218’s reported AUROC=0.859 is not treated as PRS-comparable and is further discounted because it includes strong near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) in covariates; however, PGS002766 also lacks PRS-comparable metrics and only reports an OR=1.47 (moderate) without broader validation context. With endpoint alignment broadly acceptable for both (A: incident hypothyroidism; B: hypothyroidism), the stronger overall study/validation support favors PGS005218 despite its covariate-inflated full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same disease-focused publication, with identical method (SparSNP), covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), EUR-only development/evaluation, and similar training/validation sizes—so endpoint framing and within-family performance are the main differentiators. PGS000325 shows stronger reported discrimination and effect size (full-model AUROC 0.80 [0.77–0.84], OR 1.93) than PGS000326 (AUROC 0.76 [0.72–0.80], OR 1.51). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, but given the otherwise matched design, the materially higher AUROC and OR for PGS000325 provide better-supported evidence of a stronger score than PGS000326.

PGS005266 is a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank score for Graves’ disease (a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism) with very large genome-wide coverage (1,085,170 variants; PRSCS) and broad external evaluation across multiple biobanks/ancestries (validation n=94,651; selected validation ancestry includes African American/LatAm/European). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.54), which is meaningful PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (0.664) and covariates are unknown. In contrast, PGS001043 is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less transferable; despite having clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.632, R2=0.0216, below the h2 ceiling), its endpoint is broader/self-reported hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis and its evidence package is primarily single-biobank development (UKB) with modest PRS-only performance. Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort design + stronger effect-size signal and genome-wide shrinkage structure make PGS005266 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the sparse UKB framework score.

PGS004562 has better endpoint fidelity to the target kidney failure: its phenotyping_reported is ICD code N18 (chronic renal failure), a direct kidney-failure-spectrum diagnosis, whereas PGS000708 is explicitly phenotyped as “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a restricted subtype that is less aligned to generic kidney failure. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural/effect-size evidence: PGS004562 shows a stronger per-SD effect (OR=1.395) than PGS000708 (HR=1.19), suggesting more PRS signal, and it uses a metaPRS-style integration method with much larger genome-wide variant coverage (1,059,939 vs 183,272). PGS000708’s reported C-index=0.779 is full-model (with age/sex/PCs) and not comparable as PRS performance, so it doesn’t outweigh the subtype mismatch and weaker effect size.

Both candidates align well to the target endpoint (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), but PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant count (374,114) and reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (HR 2.34, OR per SD 1.33; plus high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9) under only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), reducing risk that performance is driven by clinical packaging. In contrast, PGS000739 is a sparse 27-variant genome-wide-significant score and its reported AUROC (0.821) is explicitly from a covariate-heavy model including multiple clinical risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making the full-model AUROC less informative about PRS quality and more prone to leakage/augmentation. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either, the structural advantage (method + variant coverage) and cleaner covariate context favor PGS004911.

The two candidates are near-clones on the fields that matter most for external PRS performance: identical trait alignment (kidney cancer / renal cell carcinoma), identical endpoint (incident kidney cancer), identical ancestry (EUR GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates, identical variant count (19), and essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724) and HR per SD (1.16 vs 1.15). Candidate_b (PGS000787) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, which is a nonstandard transformation and not supported here by any PRS-only AUC/R² or incremental metrics showing improvement; its reported R²=0.366 appears to be full-model/other-metric and is not PRS-comparable (and would be implausibly high vs the provided low heritability ceiling if interpreted as PRS-only). With no clear performance advantage for the inverse-weight variant, the original GWAS-hits score (PGS000076) is the safer, better-supported choice.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity matches the umbrella disease directly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a narrower trait_efo and phenotyping_reported. Both are near-clones from the same publication, ancestry context (EUR-only dev/eval), method (SparSNP), covariates (sex, PCs 1-10), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.738 vs 0.76) are not decisive. With comparable design, the broader, target-aligned endpoint plus the stronger reported OR per SD (2.085 for PGS000114 vs 1.51 for PGS000326) favors PGS000114; the larger validation N for PGS000326 is only a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the subtype mismatch.

PGS004492 is the better-supported match to the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is cleaner: phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are ICD code N18 chronic renal failure, which aligns directly with generic kidney failure, whereas PGS000708’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a narrower subtype that is a mismatch for the broad target. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000708’s reported C-index 0.779 is a full-model metric (with age/sex/PCs) and cannot be used as standalone PRS evidence; thus performance fields don’t rescue the subtype mismatch. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural signals favor PGS004492 as well (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage with ~1.06M variants vs snpnet multi-PRS with 183k), while effect sizes are similar (OR~1.17 vs HR~1.19). Overall, PGS004492 is more likely to transfer as a general kidney failure PRS.

PGS005218 is better-supported structurally and by study archetype: it comes from a hypothyroidism-focused GWAS/prediction paper with multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), far larger training (n=1,146,562) and evaluation (n=441,692), and a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.11M variants—signals that typically transfer better than sparse single-biobank framework scores. Although its only reported AUROC is a full-model 0.859, that metric is heavily confounded by explicit near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), so it cannot be treated as PRS performance; however, candidate_b’s full-model AUROC=0.7 is also not PRS-only and comes from a portability/framework-style UKB-only SnpNet score with very sparse variant count (6,127) and unknown covariates, which is a known weaker archetype for external performance. Candidate_b does report OR=1.5 per SD (useful), but overall the disease-focused, genome-wide, multi-cohort construction of PGS005218 is more likely to rank higher than the sparse portability score despite the covariate-inflated AUC.

Both candidates match the target well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_efo and phenotyping_reported) and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R². PGS000334 reports an R²=0.191, but it is presented as a generic/full-model “proportion of variance explained” with unknown covariates and is implausibly high relative to the provided local heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), making it likely non-comparable/inflated. In contrast, PGS000053 has cleaner disclosed covariates (age, sex) and provides a PRS-relevant effect size (OR=1.29 per SD, moderate signal) plus a broader disease-focused multi-cohort development context, which is more consistent with reliable external transfer than relying on a suspect full-model R² from a C+T score.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo=osteoarthritis, knee; phenotyping_reported is knee OA/gonarthrosis) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural/study signals and effect sizes. PGS004549 has a slight edge via a multi-score aggregation-style method (RFDiseasemetaPRS, which is suggestive of combining risk-factor and disease PRS) and a larger stated development sample (n=174,489; UKB listed), with a very similar per-SD OR (~1.37) to PGS002767’s OR=1.35.
