PGS002767 has cleaner disclosed covariates (age/sex/PCs/technical) but comes from a cross-disease family-history comparison framework with no training details. Given near-tie on endpoint and OR, the method/architecture and development evidence marginally favor PGS004549, but confidence is low because covariates are unknown and no PRS-only metrics are available for either.

PGS004908 is better-supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is a direct kidney cancer PRS derived from a large, disease-focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet; 107 genome-wide significant SNPs) and shows a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58), which is a meaningful proxy for PRS discrimination when PRS-only AUC/R² are absent. PGS000787 is a pan-cancer risk-factor integration study and uses a small 19-variant score imported from another PGS with inverse weights; its PRS signal is weaker (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.24) and its reported AUROC/R² are full-model metrics with substantial non-genetic covariates, making them less informative about standalone PRS quality. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (RCC is the dominant kidney cancer subtype; incident kidney cancer is still aligned), so the stronger disease-focused construction and materially stronger per-SD effect size favor PGS004908.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R². PGS000054 has stronger PRS-relevant evidence via an explicit per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), which is a meaningful discrimination proxy when AUC/R² are missing. PGS000334’s only quantitative metric is an R²=0.191 reported as “proportion of variance explained” alongside a full-model R² field with unknown covariates; given the heritability ceiling provided (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), this magnitude is suspect/non-comparable and likely not PRS-only. With comparable validation sizes (3,324 vs 3,810) and no clear advantage from method/variant count (21 vs 22), the cleaner, interpretable effect-size evidence and basic covariates (age, sex) make PGS000054 better-supported than PGS000334.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that, PGS004860 has stronger structural support for capturing polygenic signal (LDpred2 with 1,143,554 variants) and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.33) than PGS000078 (HR=1.16), suggesting better PRS discrimination. PGS000078’s evaluation is much larger but its reported performance is heavily packaged with extensive non-genetic predictors (family history, detailed smoking variables and interactions, PM2.5), making its high full-model AUROC less informative about PRS quality; PGS004860 uses a simpler covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking/PCs), reducing covariate-driven inflation concerns.

PGS002729 is the better-supported knee osteoarthritis PRS on the visible fields because it is clearly disease-focused with a direct clinical endpoint (“Knee osteoarthritis” / “Clinical osteoarthritis”), uses disclosed and fairly standard covariates (age, sex, BMI), and is developed across multiple osteoarthritis-relevant cohorts (BBJ, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE, etc.) with an explicit European validation AUROC reported (full-model AUROC 0.66, CI 0.61–0.71; n=14,926). In contrast, PGS004549 comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”), has unknown covariates (raising comparability/packaging concerns), is single-biobank (UKB) development, and provides no discrimination metric (no AUC/R2; only a moderate OR=1.37). With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, the clearer endpoint framing and cleaner, more transparent evaluation evidence favor PGS002729.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (incident lung cancer; EFO lung carcinoma), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same variant count (109), same covariate-heavy risk-factor integration (including family history, smoking variables/interactions, PM2.5), and essentially identical reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) and HR per SD (~1.16–1.17). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly derived from candidate_a but with inverse weights, which is a strong negative structural signal for true PRS performance/transferability (it should degrade genetic signal rather than improve it), and its additional reported R²=0.799 is a full-model/unclear metric that is not PRS-comparable and is also implausibly high relative to the lung-cancer heritability ceiling context, so it should not be used to promote it. With near-clone evidence otherwise, the original correctly oriented score (PGS000078) is better-supported than an intentionally inverted-weight derivative (PGS000789).

Both candidates match the target trait (knee osteoarthritis) with EUR evaluation and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on endpoint/study archetype and whatever PRS-relevant evidence exists. PGS002729 comes from a disease-focused OA paper and shows explicit multi-cohort development (BBJ, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE, etc.) with a reported AUROC=0.66 (though full-model with age/sex/BMI, so not PRS-comparable). PGS002767 is from a cross-disease family-history vs PRS comparison framework and provides only an OR per SD of 1.35 (moderate) with no discrimination metrics; despite using a stronger genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) and many variants, the framework archetype plus limited performance reporting makes it less well-supported here. Confidence is low because PGS002767’s PRS-CS genome-wide construction could plausibly outperform the 24-SNP GWS score, but the visible record-level evidence favors the disease-focused multi-cohort OA model.

PGS000328 is better aligned to the generic target of lupus erythematosus as a disease-risk PRS: it targets systemic lupus erythematosus with a clearer disease-focused framing, whereas PGS000196’s phenotyping is explicitly restricted to “SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis,” which is a narrower, context-conditioned outpatient differential-diagnosis setting. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so the small AUROC difference (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) is weak evidence; however, PGS000328 also has a larger validation sample (n=1,001 vs n=245) and a slightly larger SNP set (57 vs 55), supporting it as the more robustly supported candidate given similar ancestry (EUR GWAS; EUR eval available for both).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo lymphoid leukemia; incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint) and use the same basic covariates and EUR-only evaluation in the same large validation sample (n=391,338). However, PGS000788 is explicitly the same 75-variant score as PGS000077 but with inverse variant weights, which is a strong red flag for biological/plausibility and likely degrades true PRS signal despite slightly higher full-model AUROC/C-index/HR reported. Since neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (and the reported AUROC/R2 appear full-model and thus not cleanly comparable), the safer, better-supported choice is the original published construction (PGS000077) rather than an inverted-weights derivative.

Both candidates are near-clones: same late-onset AD endpoint (familial LOAD), same method (21 genome-wide significant variants), same covariates (age, sex), same publication and development cohorts, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. In this near-tie, the best differentiator is the available PRS signal proxy (effect size): PGS000054 shows a materially stronger OR per SD (1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR 1.29, 1.21–1.37), which domain guidance treats as a meaningful indicator of stronger discriminative power. Although PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-only evaluation, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger reported OR for PGS000054.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration), use the same method (PRS-CS), have similar variant counts, identical basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), and are evaluated in the same EUR validation sample (n=163,011), so this is a near-clone comparison where within-family performance/effect-size differences are informative. PGS004606 shows stronger reported discrimination and PRS signal in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.71; OR per SD 1.76 [1.73–1.78]) than PGS004607 (AUROC 0.65; OR 1.48 [1.34–1.63]). Additionally, PGS004606’s GWAS ancestry (EUR) matches the EUR evaluation ancestry, whereas PGS004607 is trained on AFR-only GWAS but evaluated in EUR, a transportability mismatch that plausibly contributes to its weaker performance here.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. The key differentiator is structural PRS strength: PGS004860 uses a genome-wide LDpred2 model with 1,143,554 variants, which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal than PGS000789’s 109-variant reweighted score derived from another PGS. While PGS000789 has much heavier covariate packaging (family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking terms and interactions), making its high full-model AUROC likely covariate-driven and less informative about PRS contribution, PGS004860 uses a simpler covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking/PCs). Given similar endpoint fidelity and no PRS-only metrics, the genome-wide shrinkage construction and higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.33 vs HR 1.17) favor PGS004860 as more likely to rank higher in external PRS performance.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. Given that, PGS000077 is better-supported structurally and empirically: it uses many more variants (75 genome-wide significant hits vs 6 variants for PGS000645), shows a stronger per-SD effect size (HR 1.45 vs OR 1.358), and is evaluated in a much larger European sample (n=391,338 vs n=957). PGS000645 comes from a repository-style evaluation with very small development/training (n=1,100) and a very sparse P+T score, which is a weaker evidence package here despite having additional full-model metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication, same reported trait/EFO (melanoma), same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, and same validation sample size (n=4,765). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R²), so performance evidence is weakly comparable and small AUROC differences are likely noise. With design essentially identical, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002247 includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50) and also has marginally higher full-model AUROC/R² (0.691/0.072 vs 0.688/0.070), so it is slightly better-supported.

Both candidates are EUR-only and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS002247 is closer to the target melanoma concept with a clearly specified clinical endpoint (“incident invasive melanoma”) and uses only basic covariates (age, sex), reducing covariate-driven inflation risk. PGS000766 targets cutaneous melanoma but includes family history and treatment/interaction terms (aspirin/placebo, PRS*treatment), which are stronger packaging/leakage signals and make its full-model C-index (0.643) less comparable to standalone PRS performance. With similar sparse GWAS-hit construction, PGS002247 also shows higher reported discrimination (AUROC 0.691 vs 0.643) and slightly more variants (68 vs 56), so it is better-supported overall despite the smaller validation N.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Multiple myeloma”, EFO plasma cell myeloma), method (GWAS-significant variants), variant count (23), and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002306 (0.69 vs 0.644) is not a reliable PRS discriminator—especially since PGS002306 has unknown covariates, making that AUROC harder to interpret. PGS002281 provides cleaner evaluation context (explicit basic covariates: age/sex/region) and includes an additional PRS-relevant effect-size signal (OR highest vs lowest quintile = 3.18 [2.34–4.33]) plus a disease-focused publication specifically on MM risk prediction, whereas PGS002306 comes from a cross-cancer evaluation with less supporting detail and a much smaller validation sample (n=290 vs n=2,395).

Both candidates target systemic lupus erythematosus and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000196 (0.79 vs 0.65) is not a reliable PRS discriminator. On structural and transportability signals, PGS000754 is better-supported: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant count (293,684) and has a much larger validation sample (n=7,733) with multi-ancestry evaluation, whereas PGS000196 is a very sparse P+T score (55 variants) validated in a small outpatient arthritis setting (phenotyping: 'SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis', n=245), which is a more context-restricted endpoint. Given comparable trait mapping but stronger general-purpose PRS construction and broader validation context, PGS000754 is more likely to transfer well to a generic lupus erythematosus benchmark.

PGS000754 is better supported as a general SLE PRS for the target trait because its endpoint is the generic disease diagnosis (phenotyping_reported: systemic lupus erythematosus) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (293,684), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than PGS000328’s 57 genome-wide significant hits. Although PGS000328 shows a higher reported AUROC (0.83 vs 0.65), both candidates only report full-model AUROC (no PGS-only AUC/R2), making those values non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven; additionally, PGS000328’s phenotype is restricted to early-onset SLE (<20), which is a mismatch for the generic ‘lupus erythematosus’ target. PGS000754 also has a much larger validation sample (n=7,733 vs n=1,001) and includes European evaluation, supporting more reliable performance estimation despite its EAS-trained GWAS ancestry.

PGS000766 has stronger disease-focused development support and more informative PRS signal evidence than PGS002246. Both are EUR-only and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, making their full-model AUROC values not directly comparable as standalone PRS performance. However, PGS000766 is built from a large multi-cohort melanoma GWAS/consortium set (many listed development cohorts) and reports a per-SD HR=1.46 (moderate-to-strong discriminative signal), whereas PGS002246 provides no effect-size evidence and is primarily an independent evaluation with a smaller validation sample. Although PGS002246 uses cleaner/basic covariates (age, sex) and has a higher full-model AUROC (0.688 vs 0.643), PGS000766’s richer disease-specific development context plus explicit HR evidence outweighs the covariate-inflated full-model AUROC difference, especially given PGS000766’s heavier covariates (family history, treatment interaction) that make its full-model metric less PRS-comparable.

PGS000788 is better supported for the target trait despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R², because it shows stronger PRS signal and a more robust study context than PGS000645. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to lymphoid leukemia; PGS000788 is incident lymphocytic leukemia, a close synonym/subtype framing). On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only metrics, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable; however PGS000788 reports a strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.7), whereas PGS000645’s per-SD OR is more modest (OR=1.358), suggesting weaker standalone PRS discrimination. Structurally, PGS000788 uses many more variants (75 vs 6), and it is derived from an established leukemia PRS (Graff et al) rather than a very sparse P+T score trained/developed in a single cohort (MGI) with small training n=1,100. Although PGS000645 has a cleaner single-biobank evaluation record, its sparse construction and weaker effect size make it less likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than PGS000788.

PGS004607 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for the generic target “macular degeneration” because its endpoint is a direct AMD diagnosis (phenotyping_reported: “Age-related macular degeneration”) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and it shows a stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.48 vs 1.41 for PGS004952). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004952’s much higher reported AUROC (0.842) is only a full-model metric and not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator; additionally, PGS004952’s endpoint is narrower (“Late age-related macular degeneration”), which is a partial mismatch to the broader target. Despite PGS004607’s GWAS ancestry being AFR with EUR evaluation (a transportability concern), its genome-wide PRS-CS construction with very large variant count and stronger per-SD OR makes it more likely to rank higher than the sparse 52-SNP GWS score whose apparent advantage is driven by non-PRS-comparable full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis) and neither provides a PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS002726 is from a disease-focused MS susceptibility/phenotype study (IMSGC-based) and reports strong disease-discrimination evidence (AUROC 0.80, albeit full-model, plus a very large OR top 10% vs median = 15), which is more directly supportive of MS risk stratification than PGS002038’s portability-framework partial-r=0.0396 from a UKB-wide cross-trait portability paper. Although PGS002038 has larger training/validation and explicit basic covariates, its framework/portability archetype and weak partial-correlation signal make it less likely to rank highest in external benchmarks than the disease-focused MS score with strong effect-size evidence.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same publication (HGG Adv), same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution, and same validation sample size (n=30,379), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (only full-model C-index/AUC). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are the small performance/effect-size edges: PGS005045 shows a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.78385 vs 0.78336) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.554 vs 1.541). These differences are modest and likely within noise, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS005045 over PGS005035.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), identical variant count (1,286,612), same MVP development cohort, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model C-index differences are only a weak tie-break. On the shared European validation record, PGS005039 has slightly stronger reported performance and PRS signal (full-model C-index 0.78484 vs 0.78336; OR per SD 1.578 vs 1.541 with overlapping CIs), so it is marginally better-supported than PGS005035.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and release date, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions, and same validation sample size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model C-index is shown and is essentially identical (0.7848 vs 0.7839), so it’s not a strong differentiator. With endpoints and context matched, the small edge goes to PGS005039 because it has slightly stronger effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.578 vs 1.554) and marginally higher full-model C-index, while PGS005045 offers no compensating advantage beyond method label.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; EFO Nasal Cavity Polyp), publication, ancestry (EUR dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), training N (174,489) and validation N (56,192), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. With metrics unavailable, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS004535 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.60) than PGS004465 (1.35), which is meaningful evidence of stronger discriminative signal in the same study/endpoint context. Although PGS004465 uses LDpred2 (a strong single-score shrinkage method), within the same publication family empirical performance signals (here, OR) are the more reliable tie-break, favoring PGS004535.

PGS004606 is better supported for the generic target of macular degeneration because its endpoint is directly aligned (phenotyping_reported: age-related macular degeneration) and it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score (1,000,946 variants) with a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.76), suggesting substantial standalone PRS signal. PGS004952, while also AMD-labeled, is explicitly for a narrower endpoint (phenotyping_reported: late AMD, clinical classification) and is a sparse 52-SNP genome-wide-significant score with a weaker OR (1.41). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC reported for PGS004952 (0.842 vs 0.71) is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator; with similar basic covariates, the stronger PRS structure and effect-size evidence favor PGS004606 despite PGS004952’s higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical endpoint framing (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Tobacco use disorder; trait_efo: nicotine dependence), identical training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), identical basic covariates, and the same European-selected validation record (n=19,400), so performance is directly comparable via the reported partial correlation. PGS002037 shows materially stronger PRS signal (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (847,691 vs 13,838), which is a positive structural signal for a polygenic trait when other fields are matched. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the higher partial-r plus stronger genome-wide construction supports PGS002037 over the sparser penalized-regression score.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are “Multiple myeloma” and trait_efo is plasma cell myeloma) and both are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL with similar sparse GWAS-hit style construction (23 vs 22 variants). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; however, with similarly light covariates (PGS002281: age/sex/region; PGS000653: age/sex/PCs/batch), PGS002281 shows materially stronger discrimination and stratification in its selected validation (AUROC 0.644 vs 0.577; OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 vs OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1). PGS000653 comes from a repository/framework-style paper (Cancer PRSweb) and has only modest pseudo-R2 (0.0145) plus weaker/less stable risk separation, so PGS002281 is better-supported on the visible performance evidence without added leakage concerns.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with similar variant counts (PGS002306: 23 vs PGS000653: 22) and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL. However, PGS000653 has a clearer, better-supported evaluation package: it reports PRS-associated effect sizes (OR per SD 1.327, plus top-1% vs rest OR) and includes explicit basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), along with documented training/development cohort (UKB) and training N=3,377. PGS002306 provides only a full-model AUROC (0.69) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only metrics or effect sizes, making its apparent performance harder to interpret as PRS-driven. Given the stronger interpretability and supporting fields for PRS000653 versus covariate-uncertain full-model AUROC for PGS002306, PGS000653 is more likely to rank higher in an external benchmark.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all MS) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence). Given that, PGS000809 is better-supported because it provides clearer evaluation context (explicit basic covariates: age/sex/PCs) and includes an R² estimate (0.069) alongside AUROC=0.765, whereas PGS002726 reports only a higher full-model AUROC=0.80 with unknown covariates (harder to interpret for PRS contribution) and no R²/effect-size-per-SD. Although PGS002726 has a very large variant count and a strong top-decile OR (15.0), the lack of covariate transparency and absence of PRS-comparable metrics makes its apparent AUROC advantage less reliable than PGS000809’s more interpretable, minimally adjusted performance reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same phenotyping string (typoed but identical), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC shown, which is not a reliable differentiator). In this near-clone setting, the small but consistent empirical edge favors PGS005262: slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and stronger effect sizes (OR 1.408 vs 1.362; β 0.342 vs 0.309). Variant counts are essentially identical, and cohort lists differ only marginally, so performance/effect-size differences are the main visible tie-break.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping labels, covariates, training cohort/size, and the same multi-ancestry evaluation setup, so the main differentiators are the PRS signal metric and structural properties. PGS002033 (LDpred2, 846,292 variants) shows a higher PRS-comparable performance estimate (partial-r=0.0789 vs 0.0547 for PGS001825) in the selected European validation record, consistent with genome-wide shrinkage capturing more polygenic signal for obesity than a much sparser penalized-regression score (13,009 variants). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so partial-r plus the much broader variant coverage favors PGS002033.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (benign nodular goiter) with the same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so performance metrics are weak differentiators. In this near-clone setting, structural signals and effect sizes matter more: PGS005263 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a materially stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.36, β≈0.309) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants and much weaker effect (OR≈1.048, β≈0.047). The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.5876 vs 0.5854) is negligible. Therefore PGS005263 is better-supported and more likely to transfer as a stronger PRS.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo and same phenotyping_reported), publication family, ancestry distribution, cohort context, covariates (both unknown), and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). In this same-endpoint sibling setting, structural and effect-size evidence are decisive: PGS005262 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with 1,085,173 variants and shows much stronger per-SD association (OR=1.41, β=0.34) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T 110-variant score (OR=1.048, β=0.047). The small full-model AUROC edge for PGS005262 (0.593 vs 0.585) is consistent but secondary; overall PGS005262 is better-supported for real-world PRS performance.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so performance is hard to compare directly. PGS002038 is from a UKB portability framework paper and only provides a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.0396) with no AUROC/R²/effect-size support, which is weaker evidence for real-world ranking. PGS000809 comes from a disease-focused MS study with multi-cohort development (IMSGC and many contributing cohorts) and provides at least some discrimination/effect-size signal (full-model AUROC=0.765 with basic covariates; β=0.63), making it better-supported than the framework-derived portability score despite fewer variants.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are Osteoporosis; EUR-only evaluation) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to study archetype/covariate cleanliness and effect-size support. PGS002768 is a straightforward disease PRS (PRS-CS) with explicitly basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), avoiding risk-factor integration/packaging. PGS004565 is explicitly an integrated risk-factor + disease PRS (“Integration of risk factor polygenic risk score with disease polygenic risk score”), which is a packaging signal that often reduces standalone PRS comparability/transfer reliability, and its covariates are unknown. Effect sizes are very similar (OR ~1.31 vs ~1.33) and variant counts are similar, so the cleaner, more directly comparable PRS framing and disclosed basic covariates make PGS002768 better-supported.

PGS005235 is better supported for the target trait obesity because its endpoint fidelity is tighter: phenotyping_reported is an explicit obesity diagnosis (phecode 278.1) with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS001825 uses a broader administrative bundle (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) from a UKB portability framework. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, but PGS005235 provides a strong PRS effect-size signal (OR≈1.97 per SD), while PGS001825 only shows a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.055). Structurally, PGS005235 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) with far more variants (~710k vs ~13k), consistent with stronger capture of polygenic signal for obesity. Although PGS001825 has multi-ancestry evaluation, its framework/portability archetype plus weaker metric signal makes it less likely to rank higher than the disease-focused, diagnosis-anchored PGS005235.

Both candidates are EUR-only and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is heavily discounted and we fall back to endpoint fidelity plus structural signals. PGS000793 matches the broader target (ovarian neoplasm) better (incident ovarian cancer) but is a very sparse 36-variant score and its reported AUROC/R² are from a covariate-heavy integrated risk-factor model (includes family history and multiple reproductive/hormonal factors), making the performance evidence less informative for standalone PRS ranking. PGS003385 is a direct ovarian cancer diagnosis endpoint (serous carcinoma subtype) with much cleaner covariates (age + PCs) and a genome-wide lassosum construction with 144,810 variants, which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal and transfer better in external benchmarks than a small GWAS-hit score embedded in a risk-factor package. Subtype mismatch lowers confidence, but the cleaner PRS context and stronger method/variant coverage favor PGS003385 overall.

PGS005235 has higher endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: its phenotyping_reported is an explicit obesity diagnosis (phecode 278.1) with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader administrative bundle (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) that is less specific to obesity. Neither candidate provides PRS-comparable AUC/R2, but PGS005235 at least reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.97), which is meaningful discrimination evidence; PGS002033 only shows a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079) and no effect size. Although PGS002033 has multi-ancestry evaluation (a portability-style paper) and larger variant count, the framework/portability archetype plus weaker endpoint specificity and weaker performance signal make it less likely to rank higher than the diagnosis-anchored, effect-size-supported PGS005235.

PGS003385 is better-supported for ovarian neoplasm risk because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (lassosum) with far broader variant coverage (144,810 vs 36 for PGS000082), which is a strong structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent for both. Endpoint-wise, PGS003385 targets ovarian serous carcinoma (a major ovarian cancer subtype) while PGS000082 targets incident ovarian cancer more broadly; this is a mild mismatch but not enough to outweigh the structural advantage. Performance evidence is limited to full-model AUROC in both, but PGS000082’s covariates include family history and multiple reproductive/hormonal factors (more covariate-driven inflation risk), whereas PGS003385 adjusts only for age and PCs, making its reported AUROC/R² less confounded by clinical packaging. Both are EUR-only evaluation, and validation sizes are large but not decisive.

PGS002768 is better-supported for the target osteoporosis despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2 because it comes from a disease-focused cross-disease evaluation paper and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,091,549) and a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) in a sizable EUR validation (n=39,444) with only basic covariates. PGS001273 does report clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.5685; R2=0.00688, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework (“813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (316 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer; its PRS-only performance is also modest. With similar endpoint labeling, the framework/sparse-architecture penalty and weaker structural signal make PGS002768 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (incident pancreatic cancer; same trait_efo), ancestry (EUR eval), covariates (includes family history + BMI + smoking variables), variant count (22), and show essentially identical effect size (HR 1.49) and full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.745; C-index ~0.742–0.743). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the extra R²=0.439 in PGS000794 is likely a full-model/non-comparable metric and cannot be used as a PRS-quality advantage (and would be implausibly above the trait h2 ceiling if interpreted as PRS-only). With no clean PRS-only metrics to separate them, I default to the original GWAS-hits score PGS000083 over PGS000794, which is explicitly a reweighted/inverse-weights derivative of PGS000083 rather than an independently better-supported PRS.

PGS005217 is a disease-focused peripheral artery disease score with a clear clinical endpoint (incident peripheral artery disease) that is a close match to the target peripheral vascular disease umbrella, and it shows strong PRS signal via an HR per SD of 1.66. It is also genome-wide (LDpred2; ~1.3M variants) and validated broadly across multiple ancestries with a very large evaluation sample (n=304,294), suggesting better external robustness. In contrast, PGS001843 comes from a UKB portability framework paper (pan-trait archetype), uses a very sparse 242-variant penalized regression score, and its only reported performance is a very small partial correlation (0.0151), providing weak evidence of discriminative power despite a larger training N. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint-focused study context and effect-size evidence favor PGS005217.

Both candidates map cleanly to otosclerosis (trait_efo matches), but PGS002046 uses a generic otosclerosis endpoint while PGS001255 is explicitly time-to-event (a mild endpoint mismatch penalty). However, PGS001255 provides directly PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.6319; PGS-only R2=0.01341) under basic covariates, and these values are plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0048) without suggesting obvious inflation. In contrast, PGS002046 reports no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0182), giving weaker, less benchmark-comparable evidence of predictive strength despite its genome-wide LDpred2 construction and larger variant count. Given the need to predict likely benchmark ranking from visible support, the explicit PRS-only metrics in PGS001255 outweigh the time-to-event framing disadvantage versus the largely metric-sparse portability score PGS002046.

Both candidates target the same endpoint concept (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and both are sparse 22-variant GWAS-hit style scores with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so full-model AUROC differences are not clean PRS comparators. PGS000794’s higher full-model AUROC/C-index (0.745/0.743) is heavily discounted because its covariates explicitly include family history of cancer plus multiple smoking variables (pack-years and status), making the reported discrimination more “risk-factor package” than PRS evidence. PGS000663 is from a disease-focused pancreatic cancer risk prediction study and, while it also uses several epidemiologic covariates (including diabetes status and anthropometrics), it avoids family-history packaging and provides a directly comparable per-SD genetic effect size (OR 1.44). With near-clone genetics and no PRS-only metrics, the cleaner covariate framing and disease-focused archetype make PGS000663 slightly more likely to transfer, but the decision is close (low confidence).

PGS000902 is better-supported as a standalone PD PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with explicit multi-cohort development (23andMe/IPDGC/UKB etc.), uses more GWAS-significant variants (90 vs 44), and reports a validation discrimination metric (AUROC 0.651) albeit as a full-model metric with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). PGS003763 is framed around incident PD in a frailty-focused study and provides only a tertile HR (1.72) without PRS-comparable AUC/R2 or clear training/development details (samples_training N/A), making its PRS strength and generalizability harder to judge despite the large evaluation N.

Both candidates match the target phenotype cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all osteoporosis). However, PGS001273 is from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework paper (“across 813 traits”), using a very sparse snpnet model (316 variants) with weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5685; PGS-only R2 0.00688), suggesting limited standalone PRS signal despite clean basic covariates. PGS004565, while lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, comes from a disease-prediction study explicitly integrating disease PRS with risk-factor PRS (meta/ensemble-style; 1,059,939 variants) and reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.33), which is compatible with meaningful discrimination and avoids the typical underperformance pattern of the 813-traits sparse framework scores. Given the framework penalty and weak PRS-only metrics for PGS001273, PGS004565 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks, though confidence is tempered by missing PRS-only metrics and unknown covariates.

PGS000903 is better-supported as a standalone PD PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with explicit multi-cohort development (23andMe/IPDGC/UKB etc.), uses a much richer polygenic model (1805 variants vs 44), and reports strong discrimination evidence via effect size (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25) alongside a reported AUROC/R² (though these appear to be full-model and thus not PRS-comparable). PGS003763 is an incident-PD time-to-event application score with no training details, only 44 genome-wide significant SNPs, and only a tertile HR (1.72) without PRS-only metrics; despite its large evaluation N, its evidence package looks more like a sparse risk-stratification component than a well-validated high-performing PD PRS. Neither has PRS-only AUC/R², so structural/study-design support and effect-size strength favor PGS000903.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to the target (trait_reported ovarian cancer; trait_efo ovarian carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident ovarian cancer), share the same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (including family history), identical variant count (36), and essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC ~0.656 vs 0.66; C-index ~0.655 vs 0.654), so performance differences are negligible and not PRS-comparable anyway (no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either). In this near-clone setting, PGS000793 is explicitly a derivative re-weighting of PGS000082 (“inverse variant weights”), which is a red flag for biological/metric support rather than an independent, better-optimized PRS; it also reports an R²=0.193 that appears to be full-model/packaged and is not clearly PRS-only, making it non-decisive. Given the lack of clean PRS-only metrics and the derivative nature of candidate_b, the original disease score PGS000082 is the better-supported choice.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to psoriasis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both come from UKB-based framework/portability papers, so neither has a clear study-archetype advantage. PGS001312 provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.6916; PGS-only R2=0.0523) with basic covariates, whereas PGS002083 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.0632) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive strength harder to benchmark. Although PGS002083 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants and larger training N, the lack of directly comparable PRS metrics on the record leaves weaker visible support than PGS001312’s explicit PRS-only discrimination evidence.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match to the target trait (preeclampsia): it is explicitly trained/reported as “Pre-eclampsia” with phenotyping_reported “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” whereas PGS003587 is reported as “Gestational hypertension” (despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported and trait_efo). With no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported for either model and otherwise near-clone design (same paper, method PRS-CS, similar variant counts, same EUR evaluation and validation N, similar covariates), the tie-break is the available effect-size evidence and endpoint framing: PGS003586 shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31 vs 1.20 for PGS003587) and has the direct preeclampsia label, making it more likely to rank higher for preeclampsia.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Lancet Neurol PD GWAS meta-analysis with identical phenotype alignment (Parkinson’s disease), identical basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), same training cohorts and training N, and the same validation sample size (n=999), so the decision rests on within-family performance and structural signal. PGS000903 (C+T, 1,805 variants) shows higher reported AUROC in the selected validation record (0.692 vs 0.651 for PGS000902) and also provides additional supportive discrimination evidence (R²=0.054 and a strong OR top vs bottom quartile=6.25), whereas PGS000902 (90 genome-wide significant variants) has weaker AUROC and lacks accompanying effect-size/variance-explained metrics. With no PRS-only AUC/R² available for either, the higher AUROC plus richer supporting metrics and larger variant set make PGS000903 better-supported.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target peripheral vascular disease because it is a disease-focused PAD model with a clear clinical endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”) and provides meaningful PRS signal evidence via an HR per SD of 1.66 (strong effect-size support) plus a full-model C-index reported with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). It is also evaluated broadly across multiple ancestries with a very large validation sample (n=304,294), suggesting robustness/transportability. In contrast, PGS002055 comes from a UKB portability framework paper with a vaguer endpoint (“Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”) and only a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0175) as performance evidence, with much smaller validation (n=19,668). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint specificity and effect-size evidence favor PGS005217.

PGS003586 has substantially better endpoint fidelity to the target trait preeclampsia: its phenotyping_reported is “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia” and trait_reported is “Pre-eclampsia,” whereas PGS004593, despite mapping to preeclampsia in trait fields, has phenotyping_reported “Gestational hypertension,” which is a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either candidate, the effect-size evidence becomes more important; PGS003586 shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31) than PGS004593 (HR 1.16), suggesting higher discriminative signal. PGS003586 also has clearer disease-focused multi-cohort development metadata (multiple biobanks listed and a training n=212,034), while PGS004593 has N/A training size and no development cohorts listed, making its support less complete even though its evaluation sample is larger.

PGS005238 is the better-supported standalone PRS candidate: it is a conventional genome-wide polygenic score (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (964,607) and has evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/SAS), which is supportive for external transfer. PGS003415 is a rare pathogenic-variant model embedded in a named clinical risk calculator context (CanRisk-Prostate) with only full-model C-index reported (0.79) and no PRS-only metrics; its 268-variant rare-variant framing is less aligned with typical polygenic risk benchmarking for prostate cancer. Both are horizon-specific (5-year incident risk) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUC/C-index difference is not decisive; structural PRS properties and broader evaluation context favor PGS005238.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all psoriasis) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, so study-archetype doesn’t separate them. PGS001312 has clearly PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.6916 and PGS-only R2=0.0523 with basic covariates listed), whereas PGS001871 reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0636) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive strength harder to benchmark. Although PGS001871 has larger training N and slightly more variants, those are weak differentiators here versus having explicit PRS-only discrimination evidence; thus PGS001312 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same method/variant count (GWAS-significant, 22 variants) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. PGS000083 has a more endpoint-faithful phenotyping description (“Incident pancreatic cancer”) versus PGS000663’s horizon-conditioned framing (“0–10 years of follow-up”), which is a known packaging/endpoint penalty for generic disease-risk selection. PGS000083 also shows slightly stronger PRS signal via effect size (HR 1.49 per SD vs OR 1.44) and is supported by a much larger evaluation sample (391,491 vs 956), while PGS000663 additionally mixes in clinical/metabolic covariates (waist-to-hip ratio, diabetic status, fasting status) consistent with a broader risk-prediction package. Given similar construction, PGS000083 is better-supported for standalone pancreatic carcinoma risk.

PGS001280 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence and validation context: it reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.60765; PGS R² 0.01403) with basic covariates and these are sanity-consistent with the EUR heritability ceiling, plus it has multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) and a large training set (UKB n=269,704). In contrast, PGS003861 is disease-focused and endpoint-aligned but provides only a full-model AUROC (0.765) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its apparent performance largely non-comparable for PRS ranking; its evaluation is EAS-only with smaller validation (n=9,456).

PGS001280 is the better endpoint match to the target trait pulmonary embolism: it is explicitly PE with a PE time-to-event phenotyping (“TTE PE”), whereas PGS001277 uses a composite endpoint (“PE +/- DVT”) that mixes in deep vein thrombosis and is less phenotype-faithful to PE alone. The two scores are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet framework paper, same training cohort/size, same covariates, same ancestry distribution, same validation N), so the small PRS-only metric edge for PGS001277 (PGS-only AUROC 0.611 vs 0.608; PGS-only R² 0.0151 vs 0.0140) is modest and not enough to outweigh the cleaner PE-specific endpoint of PGS001280. Confidence is low because the designs are extremely similar and the performance differences are small.

PGS004155 is better-supported for the generic target trait “prostate cancer” because its endpoint is a direct, non–horizon-conditioned prostate cancer phenotype (phenotyping_reported: “Prostate cancer”) with no covariate packaging (covariates: 0), and it provides PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD ≈2.17) plus an R² estimate. In contrast, PGS005238 is explicitly framed as a 5-year incident risk/absolute-risk package (“5-year incident prostate cancer” with “Age-specific absolute risk adjusted by PGS relative risk”), which domain guidance flags as a strong comparability/transfer penalty; its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC (0.789) that is not PRS-comparable and is likely influenced by the risk-wrapper covariates. Despite PGS005238’s multi-ancestry GWAS and LDpred2 method, the endpoint/covariate packaging and lack of PRS-isolated metrics make it less reliable for benchmark-style PRS ranking than the cleaner disease-endpoint model PGS004155.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping (psoriasis), identical training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), identical multi-ancestry evaluation mix and validation N (n=19,615), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2. The only directly comparable performance signal shown is partial correlation in European validation, where PGS001871 is marginally higher (partial-r 0.0636 vs 0.0632 for PGS002083) with essentially identical CIs. Although PGS002083 uses LDpred2 with far more variants (71,744 vs 264), within this same-study sibling comparison the visible empirical metric slightly favors PGS001871, so it wins on the only outcome evidence provided; confidence is low because the difference is tiny and no PRS-only metrics are available.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported ("Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified"), same UKB portability publication, same training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), same covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=19,668), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. With metrics largely non-discriminating, the tie-break comes from within-family structural/performance signals: PGS002055 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (599,514 vs 242) and shows a slightly higher partial correlation (0.0175 vs 0.0151). Given identical phenotype/covariate framing, the higher-coverage shrinkage model with marginally better partial-r is better-supported than the very sparse penalized-regression score.

PGS001287 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.67648 and PGS-only R²=0.0335 (no covariates), with basic covariates listed separately, and these values are plausible under the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0028; h2_liab≈0.0735). It also has clear development context (UKB; n=269,704) and a defined evaluation record (selected validation ancestry European; n=24,905). In contrast, PGS000342 is disease-focused and endpoint-faithful (“Psoriatic arthritis”) but provides only a full-model AUROC=0.562 with unknown covariates and no PRS-only metrics/effect sizes, making its predictive strength and comparability much less supported despite the exact label match.

PGS003587 is better supported for the target trait (preeclampsia) because its endpoint fidelity is coherent: although trait_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” both trait_efo is preeclampsia and phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” matching the target diagnosis. It also comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort Nat Med study with listed development cohorts and a defined training sample (n=212,034), which is stronger transportability evidence than PGS004593’s sparse training metadata (samples_training N/A; no development cohorts listed). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size evidence is the main comparable signal; PGS003587 shows a slightly stronger per-SD association (OR 1.20) than PGS004593 (HR 1.16), while both use only basic covariates (age/PCs vs year/batch/PCs). PGS004593’s exact trait_reported label (“Preeclampsia”) and larger validation N do not outweigh its phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported = “Gestational hypertension”) and weaker study-support metadata.

PGS004155 is the better-supported standalone prostate cancer PRS: it is a genome-wide polygenic score (1,139,693 variants) with direct disease phenotyping ("Prostate cancer"), no added covariates (covariates=0), and it reports PRS-relevant effect size evidence (OR per SD ≈2.17) plus discrimination/variance metrics in evaluation. In contrast, PGS003415 is a CanRisk-Prostate 5-year incident absolute-risk package built from rare pathogenic variants (268 variants) with only a full-model C-index (0.79) and unknown covariates; the horizon-conditioned risk framing and clinical-model packaging make its reported performance less comparable to a standalone PRS and less indicative of polygenic discrimination. Validation sample sizes are similar, so the cleaner PRS structure and effect-size support favor PGS004155.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication, same endpoint (schizophrenia), same method (PRS-CS), same ancestry context (GWAS EAS+EUR; EUR-only evaluation), and same basic covariates, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family tie-break. Within this matched context, PGS000136 shows stronger reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC 0.64 vs 0.60; OR 1.7 vs 1.483) and a slightly higher variant count (833,502 vs 830,589), making it the better-supported choice despite its smaller validation N (18,461 vs 44,436), which is a weak signal.

Both candidates are UKB-derived framework/portability-style scores with broadly aligned endpoints (A: “Retinal detachment”; B: “Retinal detachments and defects”) and only basic demographic/PC covariates, so endpoint/covariate fidelity is roughly comparable. PGS001137 has clearly PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663), and its PRS-only R2 is plausible under the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0042) without suggesting obvious metric inflation. PGS002040 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 entirely and reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0276), which is harder to benchmark against PRS discrimination and provides weaker direct evidence of standalone PRS performance despite its larger variant count and training N. Given the benchmark goal and the stronger, directly comparable PRS-only metrics, PGS001137 is better-supported here.

PGS001277 has weaker endpoint fidelity (PE +/- DVT rather than PE alone) and comes from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework, but it provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.611 and PGS-only R2=0.015) with basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), and its PRS-only R2 is plausible under the EUR heritability ceiling. PGS003861 matches the target phenotype more exactly (pulmonary embolism; EAS Han Chinese) and reports a strong OR contrast, but it lacks any PRS-only AUROC/R2 and only shows a full-model AUROC=0.765 with unknown covariates, making its apparent performance non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven. Given the benchmark goal of selecting the better-supported, more reliably comparable PRS signal from visible fields, PGS001277 is the safer pick.

Both candidates align to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, but PGS001791 has stronger PRS-supporting evidence: it reports a PRS-comparable (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R2=0.005929 (PGS-only R2) in EUR evaluation and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) with ~910k variants, which is structurally better for a polygenic disease than a 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score. Its PRS-only R2 is also plausible under the provided h2_obs ceiling (0.0039) given scale differences and remains small, suggesting no obvious inflation. In contrast, PGS004695 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a high-vs-low quintile HR (3.78) from an exposure-focused cohort study with more epidemiologic covariates, making the standalone PRS contribution less directly supported and the sparse SNP set more likely to underperform in external benchmarks.

PGS001791 is better-supported for the target concept despite weaker reported PRS-only R2. Endpoint fidelity is stronger: it targets idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all aligned), which is a specific, clinically coherent subtype within pulmonary fibrosis, whereas PGS001030 is a generic “pulmonary fibrosis” phenotype from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), a study archetype noted to generalize less well. Structurally, PGS001791 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~910k variants and multi-biobank development context, which is generally more robust than the very sparse snpnet model with 51 variants in PGS001030. Although PGS001030 reports higher PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.6252; R2 0.0142 vs 0.005929), those come from the known pan-trait sparse framework setting and do not outweigh the stronger endpoint specificity and more robust genome-wide construction/transportability context of PGS001791.

PGS004163 is the better-supported choice for rheumatoid arthritis because it targets the same clinically relevant endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Seropositive RA) without the time-to-event framing that can reduce comparability for a generic RA target, and it comes from a multi-biobank evaluation/ensemble-learning context with a genome-wide, high-coverage score (778,275 variants) and strong effect-size evidence (OR per SD ≈2.46). In contrast, PGS001311 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse snpnet model (“across 813 traits”) with only 3 variants—an archetype that often generalizes poorly—and its clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.7316/0.0585) is modest and tied to a TTE endpoint. While PGS004163 lacks explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics are shown), its endpoint fidelity plus strong OR and much richer genome-wide construction outweigh PGS001311’s metric availability given the framework/sparse-model penalty.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping (“Retinal detachments and defects” mapped to retinal detachment), identical training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), identical covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation setup/validation size (n=19,445). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes reported for either, the only comparable performance signal is the selected European partial correlation: PGS002040 is higher (partial-r=0.0276, CI 0.0135–0.0416) than PGS001833 (0.0218, CI 0.0078–0.0359). Given otherwise matched context, that modest but direct metric advantage plus the more genome-wide shrinkage-style construction (LDpred2 with many variants) supports PGS002040 as more likely to rank higher.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo (rheumatoid arthritis), same phenotyping_reported (Seropositive RA), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training n=820, same ancestry distribution, same stated covariates=0, and same validation sample size (n=90,274). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we therefore rely on within-family performance/effect-size differences and structural signals. PGS004163 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) shows consistently stronger selected validation results than PGS004049 (LDpred2.CV): higher full-model AUROC (0.7469 vs 0.7283), higher R² (0.1376 vs 0.1220), and slightly higher per-SD OR (2.46 vs 2.37). Additionally, MultiPRS (ensemble/multi-score aggregation) is a positive structural signal versus a single-score method when other fields are matched. Given the shared context, these consistent advantages support PGS004163 as more likely to rank higher.

Both candidates are tightly matched on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all squamous cell carcinoma), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohort (MGI), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). In this near-clone setting, PGS000461 has slightly stronger supportive evidence: higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.491 vs 1.4) and a marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.599 vs 0.59) with similarly basic covariates. PGS000120’s larger validation sample size is only a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the stronger effect-size signal for PGS000461.

PGS005220 is better-supported for the target trait because it targets the clinically dominant subtype (obstructive sleep apnea) with explicit OSA phenotyping and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation, plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.53), which is a meaningful PRS-strength signal even without PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003213 is an ExPRSweb framework score (UKB-only EUR) with only a modest full-model AUROC (0.527) and weak effect size (OR=1.106), and its generic “sleep apnea” label does not compensate for the framework archetype and much weaker discrimination evidence. Both lack PRS-only metrics, so the stronger endpoint/study context and effect-size evidence favor PGS005220.

Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same PRS-CS method, same basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/platform/batch), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC=0.6, which is not a comparable PRS metric). In this same-endpoint sibling setting, effect size is a legitimate tie-break: PGS000133 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.691) than PGS000134 (1.483), suggesting stronger PRS signal. PGS000134 has more variants and a larger validation n, but those are weaker differentiators here given identical study family and essentially identical full-model AUROC.

PGS001030 is better-supported for the target trait (pulmonary fibrosis) because it provides clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6252; PGS-only R2=0.0142) from a defined training set (UKB; n=269,704) and includes multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), giving more directly comparable evidence of standalone PRS signal and some transportability context. Its PRS-only R2 is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling guidance (well below h2_liability). In contrast, PGS004695 is more endpoint-specific (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; incident IPF) and shows a strong quintile HR (3.78), but it lacks any PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 and has no stated training sample, making its predictive strength harder to benchmark against other PRS models despite the large evaluation N.

Both candidates are UKB-derived framework/portability-style scores with broadly aligned endpoints (A: “Retinal detachment”; B: “Retinal detachments and defects”) and similar basic covariate adjustment (demographics + PCs; no obvious clinical leakage). The key differentiator is that PGS001137 reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663), which is sanity-consistent with the trait’s low observed-scale heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.004–0.005) and provides direct evidence of standalone PRS signal. PGS001833 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 and only provides a partial correlation (0.0218), which is harder to benchmark against other PRS and offers weaker, less directly comparable discrimination evidence despite its larger variant count and training N. Given similar endpoint fidelity and study archetype, the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics makes PGS001137 better-supported here.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all match carcinoma in situ of skin), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohorts (MGI), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), training size (n=6,005) and validation size (n=5,500), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal). Although PGS000469 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with many variants, its observed discrimination/effect sizes are materially weaker here, so PGS000470 is better-supported on the visible validation evidence.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (67,425), and both report clean PRS-only AUROC/R² well below the sarcoidosis h2_liability ceiling (0.107), so heritability sanity checks don’t differentiate. Given the tiny metric differences and the endpoint mismatch risk, PGS000922 is marginally better aligned; confidence is low because the records are otherwise extremely similar and the performance gap slightly favors PGS000923.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical endpoint fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match skin carcinoma in situ), same publication family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation sample size (n=5,500). Given the same covariate set, these differences favor PGS000471 as the better-supported score.

PGS005219 is better supported for the target trait because it is a disease-focused obstructive sleep apnea score (OSA is the dominant clinical form of sleep apnea) developed/validated across multiple cohorts (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation, and it shows much stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR=1.98 per SD) than PGS003213 (OR=1.106). Although both candidates only report full-model AUROC (no PRS-only AUC/R2), PGS003213 comes from the ExPRSweb framework repository (a known weaker archetype for per-disease optimization) and its AUROC is near-null (0.527), while PGS005219’s higher AUROC (0.79) is not directly comparable due to added BMI covariate but is consistent with a stronger underlying PRS signal given the large OR.

PGS000922 is the better-supported match for the target trait sarcoidosis because its phenotype alignment is exact across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all sarcoidosis), whereas PGS001872 has a concept mismatch in trait_efo ("skin sarcoidosis") despite phenotyping_reported being generic sarcoidosis. PGS000922 also provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64282; PGS-only R2=0.01741), which is interpretable and below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.107), while PGS001872 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and reports only a partial correlation (0.0199), a weaker and less directly comparable metric. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates and similar ancestry evaluation patterns, so the decisive differences are endpoint fidelity (generic vs skin subtype in trait_efo) and availability of PRS-only metrics favoring PGS000922.

PGS004049 is the better-supported choice for generic rheumatoid arthritis risk because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2.CV) with very large variant coverage (373,627) and reports strong PRS discrimination evidence via effect size (OR per SD 2.37) on an endpoint aligned to RA (seropositive RA). Although it lacks explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R² are shown), its study context is a multi-biobank evaluation paper and its evaluation includes EUR and SAS, suggesting broader transportability than a single-cohort framework score. In contrast, PGS001311 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 3-variant model (snpnet), a structural warning sign for a complex disease; its PRS-only AUROC/R² are reported but are modest and tied to that framework setting, and the time-to-event phenotyping further reduces comparability to a generic RA endpoint. Overall, the framework+sparsity penalties for PGS001311 outweigh its cleaner PRS-only metrics, making PGS004049 more likely to rank higher externally.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. PGS000731 is better-supported on transportability/validation context: it is from a disease-focused skin cancer PRS study (Nat Commun) with a much larger European evaluation sample (n=88,924 vs n=8,473 for PGS000461), and it uses a standard PRS construction pipeline (clumping+thresholding) with a similar variant count (14 vs 13). While PGS000461 reports cleaner/basic covariates and a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.49 vs 1.44), the effect-size gap is small and does not outweigh PGS000731’s substantially broader evaluation support given the lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same method (PRS-CS), same ancestry context (GWAS EAS 6%/EUR 94%; evaluation EUR 100%), and same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, platform/batch). PGS000133’s larger validation n is a weak signal and not enough to outweigh the consistent (though modest) performance/structure edge for PGS000136.

PGS000923 is the better-supported match for the target trait sarcoidosis because its phenotype alignment is coherent (trait_efo=sarcoidosis; phenotyping_reported=TTE sarcoidosis) and it provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6456; PGS-only R²=0.018) with only basic covariates, and the PRS-only R² is plausible relative to the provided liability h² ceiling (~0.107). In contrast, PGS001872 has a notable endpoint mismatch (trait_efo=skin sarcoidosis vs target sarcoidosis) and lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R², reporting only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0199), making its predictive strength harder to benchmark despite a larger SNP count and training N. Both are UKB framework-style scores, so the decisive advantage is PGS000923’s closer trait mapping and clearer PRS-only metric evidence.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to type 1 diabetes (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.921 for PGS000024 vs 0.8508 for PGS000022) are not cleanly comparable PRS metrics. Given that limitation, PGS000024 is better-supported structurally and contextually: it uses more variants (85 vs 37) with additional interaction modelling (vs simple genome-wide significant variants), is developed in a disease-focused consortium cohort (T1DGC listed, whereas PGS000022 has no training cohort listed), and has much broader evaluation ancestry coverage and far larger validation sample size (n=374,000 with multiple ancestries vs n=1,447). With no PRS-only metrics to anchor ranking, these combined signals favor PGS000024 over PGS000022.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all match carcinoma in situ of skin), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohorts (MGI), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), training N (6,005) and validation N (5,500), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so we must lean on within-family empirical performance/effect sizes rather than method labels or variant count.
