Given identical covariates, these differences likely reflect a stronger PRS contribution for PGS000471, outweighing PGS000469’s larger genome-wide variant count.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Thyroid cancer” / thyroid carcinoma), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and publication family, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. In this same-context comparison, PGS000631 shows consistently stronger performance signals: higher AUROC (0.636 vs 0.618), higher pseudo-R² (0.0478 vs 0.0365), better Brier (0.0803 vs 0.0812), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.651 vs 1.568). Although PGS000632 has a larger training/validation sample and a higher top-1% OR, those are weaker tie-breakers here than the overall discrimination/effect-size pattern favoring PGS000631.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Thyroid cancer”, trait_efo thyroid carcinoma), same method (GWAS Hits), same variant count (10), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) from the same publication family. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the best differentiators are the within-family performance/effect-size signals and evaluation context. PGS000631 shows consistently stronger reported discrimination/effect sizes in its selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.626; Nagelkerke R² 0.0478 vs 0.0393; OR per SD 1.651 vs 1.598; top 1% vs rest OR 4.4 vs 3.53), while keeping similarly clean covariates and EUR evaluation. PGS000630 has a larger validation sample and includes a mixed EUR/MAE evaluation distribution, but that breadth is modest and its performance signals are weaker; validation size is a weak tie-break. Therefore PGS000631 is better-supported to rank higher.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same endpoint fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all thyroid cancer/carcinoma), same training cohort (MGI), same training N (4,481), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation sample size (n=4,270). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot prefer on clean PRS-comparable metrics. In this same-context comparison, PGS000630 has slightly better overall discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.626 vs 0.618; Nagelkerke R² 0.0393 vs 0.0365; per-SD OR 1.598 vs 1.568), while PGS000632’s higher top-1% OR (5.14 vs 3.53) is a single tail metric that doesn’t outweigh the consistently slightly stronger central metrics for PGS000630. Differences are small, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same obstructive sleep apnea endpoint (phenotyping_reported), same EFO mapping, same publication/study family (FinnGen/MGBB/MVP), same covariates (including BMI), same evaluation ancestry and validation N, and both only report a full-model AUROC=0.79 (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so AUROC cannot differentiate PRS strength. The main differentiator is effect size: PGS005219 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR=1.98 (1.74–2.24) versus PGS005220 OR=1.53 (1.39–1.68), which is meaningful evidence of stronger PRS discrimination within the same context. The AdjustedBMI vs UnadjustedBMI label does not change the endpoint fidelity here, so the stronger OR makes PGS005219 better-supported.

PGS001781 is better-supported for a generic T2D PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with substantially broader variant coverage (1,091,673 vs 555,528) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation breadth (AFR/AMR/ASN/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS) rather than the more limited EUR+GME evaluation in PGS003114. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model AUROCs (0.852 for PGS001781 vs 0.825 for PGS003114) are not decisive; however, PGS001781 also reports a plausible per-SD OR=1.52 supporting meaningful PRS signal without obvious clinical-covariate leakage (both use only basic demographics/PCs/array/batch). PGS003114 is from an ExPRSweb framework/repository context, which is a negative archetype signal versus the more disease-focused T2D risk-factor integration study in PGS001781.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS000024 uses a much richer score (85 variants with interaction modelling) versus PGS000023’s very sparse 7-variant GWAS-hits score, which is less likely to capture polygenic signal. PGS000024 is also trained on EUR GWAS (more aligned with the selected European validation record) and has broader evaluation ancestry representation and a much larger stated validation sample size (374,000 vs 57,643), while PGS000023 is AFR-GWAS-derived and may underperform in EUR evaluation. The higher full-model AUROC in PGS000024 (0.921 vs 0.817) is only weak support, but it is directionally consistent with the stronger model structure.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (T2D in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.793 for PGS002308 vs 0.825 for PGS003114) are not decisive or directly comparable. PGS002308 is better-supported structurally and for external transfer: it comes from a disease-focused trans-ancestry T2D PRS development/validation study, uses PRS-CSx with substantially broader genome-wide coverage (1,259,754 variants vs 555,528), and shows explicitly diverse evaluation ancestries (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME) rather than the ExPRSweb framework context of PGS003114. While PGS003114 reports a larger OR per SD (3.959 vs 1.96), its framework/repository archetype and EUR-only GWAS/development make that apparent advantage less reliable for generalizable performance than the multi-ancestry, disease-focused design of PGS002308.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Ulcerative colitis”) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). PGS001306 has the key advantage of reporting clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.630 and PGS-only R²=0.02036), which also pass the heritability ceiling sanity check (well below h2_liability≈0.2646). PGS001855 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² and only reports partial correlation (0.0625), making its predictive strength less directly supported/comparable here despite larger training N and more variants. Because both are similar study archetypes, the presence of explicit PRS-only performance evidence tips the decision to PGS001306, but confidence is low given cross-metric incomparability and missing AUC/R² for PGS001855.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all squamous cell carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is only weakly informative. PGS000731 has slightly stronger effect-size evidence (OR 1.44, tighter CI 1.41–1.48) than PGS000120 (OR 1.40, CI 1.31–1.50), a modestly higher full-model AUROC (0.605 vs 0.59), more variants (14 vs 10), and much larger validation (n=88,924 vs n=20,468). PGS000120’s advantage is cleaner disclosed basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch) versus unknown covariates for PGS000731, but without any PRS-only metrics this is not enough to outweigh PGS000731’s consistently stronger performance/effect-size signals in the same EUR evaluation context.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication (Cancer PRSweb), with identical trait alignment (Bladder cancer / urinary bladder carcinoma), identical phenotyping_reported (Cancer of bladder), identical EUR-only training/evaluation context (UKB; n=12,992 training; n=13,530 validation), and the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-only metrics. In this same-endpoint, same-covariate setting, the small but consistent performance/effect-size advantages favor PGS000613: higher full-model AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher pseudo-R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), stronger top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284). Given the near-identical design, these within-family differences are the best available tie-break, making PGS000613 better-supported than PGS000611.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and similarly basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs). However, PGS001306 is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (179 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external performance despite having explicit PRS-only AUROC/R² (PGS-only AUROC 0.630, R² 0.020). PGS004253 comes from a disease-focused UC study context and uses genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2-auto) with far broader variant coverage (744,575) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.84), which is a strong predictor of real-world PRS discrimination; its reported AUROC (0.66) is full-model only, so less directly comparable, but it is not driven by heavy clinical covariates. Given the framework penalty and extreme sparsity for PGS001306 versus the disease-focused, genome-wide LDpred2-auto construction and strong OR for PGS004253, PGS004253 is better-supported to rank higher externally.

Both candidates match the target trait (T2D) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS001781 (0.852 vs 0.793) is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator. PGS002308 is better-supported structurally and for transportability: it is explicitly a trans-ancestry T2D PRS using PRS-CSx with multi-ancestry GWAS input and broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME), whereas PGS001781 is trained on EUR-only GWAS and comes from a risk-factor integration paper with an incident-only endpoint, making its strong full-model AUROC more likely to be covariate/context dependent. PGS002308 also shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.96 vs 1.52), which is a more PRS-relevant signal than full-model AUROC when PRS-only metrics are absent.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (Type 1 diabetes; trait_efo matches) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, with covariates unknown), so the full-model AUROC difference is not a clean PRS discriminator. In that setting, structural signals matter more: PGS000022 uses the same GWAS-hits method but includes substantially more variants (37 vs 7), which is generally favorable within the same method family for capturing more polygenic signal. PGS000023 has broader/more diverse evaluation and much larger validation N, but validation size is a weak tie-break and the multi-ancestry evaluation does not compensate for the much sparser variant set when PRS-only metrics are absent. Therefore PGS000022 is better-supported to rank higher.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same PRSweb paper with identical endpoint mapping (trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), identical EUR-only ancestry context, and the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.571 vs 0.572) is essentially noise. In this tie-like setting, PGS000613 is better-supported: it has a stronger top-1% vs rest risk separation (OR 2.91 vs 1.47) and a better Brier score (0.0821 vs 0.0917), with similar per-SD OR (~1.30) between the two. Method/structure also mildly favors PGS000613 (P+T with slightly more variants: 15 vs 13) without introducing extra covariate leakage. Overall, PGS000613 has the more convincing performance signals given otherwise matched design.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/EFO and phenotyping (“Cancer of bladder”), same method (GWAS Hits) with the same 13 variants, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, and identical basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) from the same publication family. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.567 vs 0.572) are weak tie-breakers. PGS000611 has stronger risk stratification evidence (OR top 1% vs rest 2.66 vs 1.47) and slightly tighter per-SD effect size precision (similar OR but smaller SE for beta), while PGS000610’s small AUROC edge is likely noise in this context. Therefore PGS000611 is marginally better-supported, but the decision is low-confidence due to high similarity and lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS001250 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance for this urolithiasis target: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R² 0.00592, no covariates) on a closely aligned endpoint (calculus of kidney and ureter; nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis). In contrast, PGS001864 has no PRS-only AUC/R² and only a small partial correlation (partial-r 0.0323), which is weaker and less directly comparable as a discrimination metric. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (urinary calculus/urolithiasis spectrum), covariates are similarly basic, and both are UKB framework-style scores; while PGS001864 has more variants and slightly larger training N, those structural advantages are not enough to outweigh PGS001250’s clearer, directly interpretable PRS-only performance evidence.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its endpoint context is disease-focused (publication explicitly about autoimmune vitiligo and polygenic inheritance) and its evaluation appears aligned to vitiligo status, whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly treatment/setting-specific (anti‑PD‑L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients), a clear endpoint mismatch/therapy-induced proxy for generic vitiligo risk. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS000738 at least reports a pseudo R² (0.0386) and a beta, while PGS000760 provides only an HR (1.41) plus a meta-analysis p-value, with performance not directly comparable to vitiligo risk prediction. Both are EUR-only, so ancestry doesn’t differentiate; despite PGS000760’s larger training N, endpoint fidelity dominates, favoring PGS000738.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported (Urinary calculus), same trait_efo (urolithiasis), same UKB portability publication, identical training sample size (n=391,124), identical covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=19,913). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best differentiators are the comparable PRS metric available (partial-r) and structural properties. PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (0.0385 vs 0.0323) and is a genome-wide shrinkage score with far more variants (731,196; LDpred2) versus PGS001864’s much sparser penalized regression score (5,599 variants). Given identical endpoint/covariates/publication family, the higher partial-r plus broader genome-wide coverage supports PGS002075 as more likely to rank higher.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its endpoint is directly vitiligo (phenotyping_reported: “TTE vitiligo”) and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R²=0.01621), with basic covariates and a large validation sample (n=67,425). Its PRS-only R² is also well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.17), making the metric plausible. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major endpoint mismatch: phenotyping_reported is “anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients,” which is not vitiligo, and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² (only an HR=1.41 in a small validation n=1,584). Despite PGS001536 coming from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a known generalization risk), the direct phenotype alignment plus explicit PRS-only metrics outweigh PGS000760’s off-target phenotype and sparse performance evidence.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and neither reports a PRS-only AUROC/R2, so performance comparability is limited. PGS004253 is from a disease-focused UC study and provides supportive PRS signal via a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.84, 95% CI 1.76–1.93) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575), which is structurally favorable for a polygenic disease. PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability/framework paper with a very sparse model (1,505 variants) and only a modest partial correlation (0.0625) as its main metric; despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger training/validation Ns, framework-style sparse scores are less reliably top-performing in external benchmarks when a disease-focused, genome-wide score with strong effect-size evidence exists.

PGS001795 is better-supported for uterine cancer risk as a standalone PRS: it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) with basic demographic+PC covariates and very large European evaluation (n=170,276). That PRS-only R2 is also plausible under the provided EUR heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability h2≈0.0116), suggesting no obvious metric inflation. In contrast, PGS000541 is a sparse 18-variant GWAS-hits score with only full-model AUROC reported (0.576) and no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its PRS contribution hard to compare; its evaluation sample is much smaller (n=6,987). Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (uterine cancer / malignant neoplasm of uterus), so the combination of genome-wide method/coverage plus explicit PRS-only performance evidence and broader validation favors PGS001795.

PGS001536 is better-supported as a vitiligo PRS on the visible fields: it has endpoint-aligned phenotyping (“TTE vitiligo” / vitiligo time-to-event) and reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R²=0.01621), with basic covariates only (age, sex, PCs, array) and a large, clearly described UKB development/validation setup. Its PRS-only R² is also plausible under the vitiligo h2_obs ceiling (~0.17). In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata incoherence (phenotyping_reported = “Red hair” despite trait_reported/EFO = vitiligo), lacks PRS-only AUROC/R², and only provides a pseudo-R²/full-model-style metric with unknown covariates, making its evidence less directly supportive for vitiligo risk prediction despite being from a disease-focused paper.

PGS003381 is better-supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint is a clinically dominant subtype match (endometrial carcinoma/endometrial carcinoma; phenotyping_reported: uterine endometrial carcinoma), which domain guidance treats as strongly aligned to uterine cancer, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (529,365) and a much larger European evaluation sample (n=144,479). In contrast, PGS000541 is an exact-label uterine cancer endpoint (malignant neoplasm of uterus) but comes from a repository/framework-style paper and is a very sparse GWAS-hits score (18 variants) with modest full-model AUROC (0.576) and smaller evaluation (n=6,987). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the large full-model AUROC difference is not treated as a clean PRS comparison; the structural/method + dominant-subtype endpoint support favors PGS003381.

PGS001795 is the better-supported choice for the target trait “uterine cancer” because its endpoint matches the umbrella trait directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Uterine cancer”), whereas PGS003381 targets the dominant subtype “uterine endometrial carcinoma” (strong but still narrower than the target). Critically, PGS001795 reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2 / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R² = 0.001948), which is interpretable against the provided low heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability≈0.0116) and indicates some standalone PRS signal; PGS003381 provides only full-model AUROC/R² (0.761/0.11) with no PGS-only metric, so its apparent performance is not directly attributable to the PRS. Both use only basic demographic/PC covariates and EUR evaluation, so the deciding factors are the direct phenotype alignment plus the presence of PRS-only performance evidence in PGS001795.

PGS002075 is the stronger pick for the target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct generic diagnosis-style phenotype (“Urinary calculus” / “Urinary calculus”) aligned to urolithiasis, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (731,196), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001250 (341 variants). Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R² 0.00592), it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), which is a negative generalization signal, and its time-to-event endpoint framing (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”) is a mild mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target. PGS002075 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R², but it provides multi-ancestry evaluation context and a PRS-comparable partial correlation (partial-r 0.0385) without obvious clinical-risk packaging; combined with better endpoint fidelity and method/coverage, it is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking than the sparse framework score.
